entry.title: SAP Document AI Workspace: Features You Need to Know
entry.content:
This blog is a comprehensive guide to navigating the Workspace UI — from document uploads and schema configuration to channels, workflows, and transport management.

The SAP Document AI Workspace is the new, full-featured environment for all document processing tasks on SAP BTP. From now on, all the latest SAP Document AI features are available exclusively in the Workspace UI — making it the recommended starting point for every new project involving document extraction, validation, and automation.

What Can You Do in the Workspace?

The SAP Document AI Workspace handles a wide range of activities throughout the document extraction lifecycle. It provides a centralized interface that reduces operational complexity, enhances process transparency, and accelerates deployment of document AI solutions across enterprise environments.

 

👤User Menu

The User Menu in the top-right corner of the Workspace lets you personalize your experience. From here you can change the display language (34 languages are supported), adjust UI theme options, and switch between client configurations.

💡 Tip: The Workspace supports localization in over 34 languages, making it accessible for global enterprise rollouts without additional configuration.

 

📂All Documents

The All Documents screen is your central hub for managing every document uploaded to the Workspace. It supports viewing, filtering, sorting, editing, and exporting, giving you full visibility across the extraction lifecycle.

Documents move through statuses: PENDING → PROCESSING → DONE (or flagged for manual review). Once confirmed, extracted data can be exported or pushed downstream to connected SAP systems.

🧩 Schemas

Schemas are at the heart of SAP Document AI. They define which fields to extract from a given document type — both header-level fields and line-item fields. The Workspace lets you view, enable, create, configure, and activate schemas.

SAP provides pre-trained schemas for common business documents including invoices, purchase orders, remittance advices, and more. For anything beyond these, you can build custom schemas leveraging Generative AI and LLMs — no template maintenance required.

✨ Instant Learning: As users confirm or correct extractions in the Workspace, the model learns immediately via few-shot prompting — improving accuracy on the next run without a separate training cycle.

 

📡Channels

The Channels feature manages how documents enter and leave the Workspace automatically. Inbound channels can monitor email inboxes (including Microsoft Exchange/Outlook via Azure app registration), while outbound channels handle notifications and API callbacks to downstream systems.

  • Inbound Email Channel: Register an Azure app with Mail.ReadWrite permissions, then map a specific email folder to a target schema in the Workspace.
  • Automatic Ingestion: When a document arrives in the monitored inbox, the Workspace extracts it according to the configured schema — no manual upload needed.
  • Outbound Callbacks: Configure webhook endpoints to push confirmed extraction results directly to SAP S/4HANA, SAP Build Process Automation, or any external system.

⚠️ Note: Email channel configuration requires an Azure AD application registration with appropriate mail permissions and a trust setup in your SAP BTP subaccount.

⚙️Workflows

Workflows let you automate complex, multi-step document processing tasks by chaining together the core Workspace capabilities. They can be triggered automatically via inbound channels — such as incoming emails — or invoked programmatically via the OData V4 API.

For example, a workflow can automatically extract data from an uploaded income statement, pass it to SAP Build Process Automation for business-rule evaluation, and create a Sales Order in SAP S/4HANA Cloud — all without manual intervention.


 


🚀Transports

The Transports feature integrates the Workspace with SAP Cloud Transport Management, enabling you to move schemas, workflows, and channel configurations across environments (development → test → production) in a governed, traceable way.

Schemas and model versions are first-class transport artifacts: they are versioned, can be activated or rolled back independently, and are fully transportable — reducing risk when promoting changes to production.

 

🛠Settings

The Settings menu contains configuration options that apply globally across all Workspace features. Key settings include:

⭐Best Practices & Key Takeaways

  • Use the Workspace UI for all new projects. The classic Basic UI will not receive new features going forward — all innovation is Workspace-only.
  • Subscribe using the -ias application plan when setting up entitlements in SAP BTP, as this provisions the Workspace interface.
  • Document quality matters. Invest in good scanning practices — OCR accuracy and extraction quality are directly tied to input file quality.
  • Design for human-in-the-loop. Even with high confidence scores, include a review step for business-critical data.
  • Leverage Instant Learning. Confirm or correct documents regularly to continuously improve extraction accuracy without retraining.
  • Use Transports for lifecycle management. Never configure production schemas manually — use the transport pipeline.

entry.title: Can AI Tell Your FI Ticket from Your MM Ticket? Does BYOM (Bring Your Own Model) helps?
entry.content:
The Problem: Which SAP Team Should This Ticket Go To?

If you've spent any time in an SAP support team, you would have lived this moment: a ticket lands with a subject like "PO stuck, please help urgently" via email or SNow and no indication of whether it's a Materials Management problem, a Finance problem, or a Integration Suite (CPI) interface quietly failing in the background. Someone, like us (SAP Full-Stack Developer) usually a lead/senior con has to read it, guess the module, and reroute it. Multiply that by a few hundred tickets a month and you've got a real cost hiding in plain sight. 

This is not a intro story, it is my real time experience I've had in work place.

Image generated by AI: Prompt: Can you create image for The Problem: Which SAP Team Should This Ticket Go To?

That is the question behind sap-ticket-classifier-bert: can a BYOM self sufficient, purpose-built AI model handle that first triage step instead of a person? Try it right now:

  • Live demo: https://HeisenbergLupenix-sap-ticket-classifier-app.hf.space/
  • Model card: https://huggingface.co/HeisenbergLupenix/sap-ticket-classifier-bert

Why "Just Use ChatGPT" Isn't Enough

"Don't use a sledgehammer to crack a nut." It's tempting to point a large general-purpose LLM at every problem, but ticket routing is a narrow, repetitive, high-volume classification task, exactly the case where a small fine-tuned model beats a giant one on cost, latency, and predictability. You don't need a model that can write poetry to know that "GR/IR mismatch on vendor invoice" is an FI ticket. You need something fast, cheap to run, and consistent.

Here I propose BYOM (Bring Your Own Model) which can avoid huge token cost, and client specific data driven solution. 

const message = `AI Ethics & Responsibility: Think once again before using ChatGPT.
Estimates suggest that few conversations with ChatGPT may be associated with about 
500 mL (half a litre) of drinking water used for data center cooling.`;

console.log(message);

So the approach here is: take bert-base-uncased known open source base model,  add a classification head of neural networks, and fine-tune it specifically on SAP support ticket language.

Refer the technical details in the model card. 

Figure 1: SAP ticket classification flow using a fine-tuned BERT model

Nine buckets, one blind spot solved

The model sorts tickets into nine categories: FI, MM, SD, HR, ABAP, BASIS, INTEGRATION, OTHERS, and UNKNOWN.

That INTEGRATION category is the one most home-grown ticket systems get wrong. Middleware issues,

  • A CPI iFlow failing, an IDoc stuck in status 51,
  • An OData service timing out - don't cleanly belong to any one functional module, so they get bounced around before landing with the right team.

Giving integration its own first-class category means those tickets get to the CPI/PI team immediately instead of on the third handoff.

How well does it actually work?

On held-out test data, the model hits 82.4% overall accuracy and an 82.6% weighted F1 score. Some categories are close to solved, HR, INTEGRATION, and UNKNOWN tickets are classified correctly more than 94% of the time. The harder categories are MM and SD, sitting around 60–70% F1, which honestly matches reality: a lot of tickets genuinely straddle both (a delivery pricing issue touches MM and SD at once), so some confusion there isn't a bug, it's the nature of the taxonomy.

The part that matters more than the accuracy number

Any model trained on a small seed dataset will make mistakes once it meets real-world tickets. So the demo isn't a one-shot prediction tool — it has a built-in correction flow. When the model gets something wrong, you tell it the right answer on the spot. Those corrections get folded back into training with extra weight, so the model is continuously nudged toward the mistakes it's actually making, not hypothetical ones.

That loop : predict, correct, retrain. It is the difference between a cute demo and something you'd trust to sit in front of a real ticket queue.

Try it on your own tickets

Paste any ticket text into the live demo and watch it break down confidence across all nine modules. Or call it directly for inference. 

Try out - Colab

from transformers import pipeline

clf = pipeline(
    "text-classification",
    model="HeisenbergLupenix/sap-ticket-classifier-bert",
    revision="v0.2",
    top_k=None,
)

result = clf("Vendor invoice not posted due to GR/IR account mismatch")
# [{'label': 'FI', 'score': 0.93}, {'label': 'MM', 'score': 0.03}, ...]

top = max(result[0], key=lambda x: x['score'])
print(top["label"], top["score"])   # FI  0.93

Where this goes next

The current version is trained on 369 examples,  enough to prove the concept, not yet enough for blind production trust. The next step is fine-tuning it on real, anonymized ticket history from live SAP CIG/CPI integration work, which should push accuracy up meaningfully on the trickier MM/SD boundary cases.

If your team is sitting on years of SAP ticket history and still routing tickets by hand, this is a small proof that you don't need a massive model to fix that, you need the right labels, a focused model, and a feedback loop that keeps it honest.

The solution to this problem is "SAP Support Ticket Classifier — Arinous-0.2"  it identifies the correct team and owner for a ticket automatically. Try it.

Figure 2: Bring Your Own Model (BYOM) Arinous-0.2 deployed in HuggingFace

entry.title: Solving the Last Mile of Invoice-to-PO Line Matching in SAP MM & FI. Does traditional ML help here?
entry.content:
The Problem: A Month-End Nightmare

While working with an accounts payable team, I watched month-end turn into a nightmare in a PO-based MIRO world. Every open supplier invoice has to post before the books close, and leadership watches blocked and unmatched invoices like a Canis-Lupus.

So as the SAP specialist on the ground, I dug in. Turns out a big chunk of those stuck invoices had nothing to do with price or qty variance. They simply had no safe way to match invoice lines to PO line items  the invoice didn't mirror the PO's structure, the vendor never referenced PO line numbers, and SAP had nothing to propose a clean match from.

So it fell to a person. Invoice open on one screen, MIRO on the other, manually mapping every line to the right PO or GR before the system would even let it through. Multiply that by a stack of invoices at month-end, and a "standard" process turns into a grind nobody signed up for.

ChatGPT-Prompt: Can you please generate image for The Problem: A Month-End Nightmare in SAP MIRO, PO Invoice 2 PO Matching.

The Invoice Already Knows the PO. Just Not the Line.

Here's the thing nobody outside AP really understands about this problem: the invoice does tell you which PO it belongs to. UBL 2.1 and Peppol BIS 3.0 e-invoices carry the PO reference right there in the header 

<cac:OrderReference>PO-4500067890</cac:OrderReference> 
(OR)
<cbc:BuyerReference>PO-4500067890</cbc:BuyerReference>

So SAP knows the invoice is against PO-4500012345, PO-4500067890, and PO-4500099001.

What it doesn't know is which of the dozens of lines across those three POs each invoice line actually maps to. That mapping only exists at the header level. Line-level PO references are technically possible in the standard  I've seen maybe one vendor in the wild actually populate them. Everyone else leaves you to figure it out.

And "figure it out" usually means a human, squinting at two descriptions:

Invoice says

PO says

Hex Bolts M10

Hex Head Bolt M10x50mm Grade 8.8

Office Paper A4 500 sheets

A4 Copy Paper Ream 500

Same item. Zero words in common that matter. A junior AP clerk gets this right in about two seconds. A rules engine built on exact-match or Levenshtein distance gets it wrong every time, because the problem was never spelling  it's meaning.

  • Live demo: https://karthionlupenix-invmatchmaker.hf.space

Why Not Just Call an LLM?

The obvious answer today is "just call an LLM." It would probably match "Hex Bolts M10" to "Hex Head Bolt M10x50mm Grade 8.8" just fine if you asked it nicely. But an LLM call per invoice line, multiplied by every candidate PO line, across every invoice a company processes in a month, is slow and expensive for what is fundamentally a narrow, repetitive, high-volume matching task  not a reasoning task. You don't need something that can write you a poem to know two part descriptions refer to the same bolt.

Traditional machine learning doesn't get the hype right now. But for "does this invoice line mean the same thing as this PO line," it's the right tool, not the consolation prize.

The Practical Approach

The knowledge I picked up from University of Auckland's MAI course and Stanford's Machine Learning course pointed me toward a Feature ranking approach. This isn't a full AP automation suite there are enough of those already, and most are still doing header-level three-way match dressed up as "AI." I built specifically the part that's missing: given an invoice and the POs it already references, which PO line does each invoice line belong to.

Detailed Technical related content has mentioned in the below link with coding: 

The Invoice Already Knows the SAP PO. Artificial Intelligence Finds the Right Line.

Why This Instead of Buying Something Off the Shelf

Most AP automation platforms are excellent at OCR and header-level tolerance matching, and I have no interest in rebuilding that. What they're mostly not built for is this specific line-level semantic step Rossum's own PO-matching extension, for instance, checks whether line items match by ID and field overlap, not by meaning. That's the gap this sits in: not a capture tool, not a three-way match engine, just the piece that answers "which line" once the header-level "which PO" is already known.

Related Work
This isn't the first attempt at line-level semantic matching. A 2020 paper, Online Similarity Learning with Feedback for Invoice Line Item Matching (arXiv:2001.00288), tackled the same gap using NER and taxonomy-based Jaccard similarity with a human-feedback loop, rather than embeddings. It's worth a read if you want to see how this problem was approached before Sentence-BERT-style models made semantic similarity cheap and fast.

Try It

If your team is still doing this matching by hand and you're curious what a semantic-first approach looks like on real SAP MM fields, the MVP is live invoice XML in, SAP-ready IDoc XML out, nothing hidden behind a demo request form.

Live demo and docs linked below. This is a Phase 1 proof of concept feedback on where it breaks is genuinely more useful to me than praise.

entry.title: SAP AI Adoption & Learning Week – Day 3 in review
entry.content:
In my Day 2 recap, I showed what the Autonomous Enterprise looks like in Finance, CX, and Supply Chain.  All of it runs on one foundation: the SAP Business AI Platform. This is where agents get built, where they get context, and where they get governed. Day 3 was for the builders: the developers, architects, and technical consultants who turn this vision into reality.

Here's my recap of the day's sessions and the questions that came up most.

The morning briefing (recording) started with a provocative question: Is AI the new plastic? AI is the most overrated and underrated technology at the same time. Some people don't use it where they should. Others use it for everything without understanding its limitations or how to design these systems well. Plastic works the same way. It's an incredible material in medicine, and completely absurd when used to wrap a banana that already has a peel.

The message for Day 3: build AI intentionally. Know where it adds real value and if you're building agents, build the evaluation framework alongside them.

This is what we then saw in the new, fully managed Joule Studio, planned for general availability in Q3 2026. It introduces intent-based development: describe what you want to accomplish in natural language and Joule Studio guides the journey from business intent to production-ready agent. For example: We process 50,000 invoices each month with a team of 10. Most delays are due to matching issues and invoices being routed to the wrong approver. I'm looking for an automated solution. With one prompt, the agent handles classification, matching, routing, and exception escalation autonomously. Rewatch Step-by-step guidance to build custom Joule agents in Joule Studio to see how.

Answers to your most asked questions:

  • When is Joule Studio GA and how do I get access?
    GA is planned for end of Q3 2026. The Early Adopter Care program has started and registration is now closed. Trial access is being planned.
  • What happens to Joule Studio Classic?
    Joule Studio Classic continues with a free promotion as part of SAP Build. A migration path to the new, fully managed SAP Joule Studio is available that automatically converts your existing agents and skills into the new format which is the recommended path.
  • Do I need a technical background to use it? The intent-based development is designed for different levels of technical experience. Joule chat guides you through the entire solution or code generation with natural language.

The invoice demo in Joule Studio was no coincidence. Unstructured documents such as invoices, contracts, delivery notes, and quality certificates are where enormous amounts of business value get stuck. SAP Document AI (recording) is built to unlock them.

Did you know about the recent and upcoming feature releases in SAP Document AI?

  • Inbound and outbound channel support, which enables you to fetch the e-mail, extract both the e-mail body and attachments, such as Excel files. Follow the documentation to register an e-mail app here.
  • Standard extraction supports most document fields. But what about the ones specific to your business? With custom prompting you can write your extraction rules in plain language, choose your model, and combine with built-in extraction in the same schema. (Planned for Q3/2026)
  • With everyone talking about agents, how can agentic AI help with document processing? Agentic workflows shift document processing from a tool that reads to an agent that can reason and act when validating a payment advice note. (Planned for Q3/2026)

Answer to your most asked question:

  • What file types and document formats are supported?
    It depends on your license. The base edition covers the most common business document types. The premium edition extends to additional formats CSV, for example, is not included in the base edition. The full list is in the SAP Help documentation.

Custom prompting in SAP Document AI already hinted at it: you choose your model, you write your rules. That flexibility raises a bigger question: how do you access, evaluate, and govern all the models available to you across your entire AI landscape? That's what the session Build Your Own AI Solution with Generative AI hub answered. Rewatch it here.

Generative AI hub gives you access to leading frontier models like GPT-5.5, Claude 4.8 Opus, Gemini 3.5 Flash, Mistral Small 4, and SAP's own foundation models. The platform is built around one core insight: the best AI is not one model. Different tasks need different intelligence. The Evaluation Service is how you find the right fit and benchmark any model against your own data and metrics. Get started by finding the right model for the right task: first, find a use case that is visible and impactful. Then experiment, start small, iterate fast, and learn what works. Finally, operationalize, build the framework, define standards, and share what you've learned across your organization. Try it yourself with the free 30-day trial or continue with the on-demand CodeJam hands-on exercise “Getting started with Generative AI Hub on SAP AI Core” on GitHub.

Answers to your most asked questions:

  • Where can I find the full list of supported models?
    See SAP Note 3437766 and the SAP Road Map Explorer for the latest model catalog, regional availability, and input/output token details. Use the Generative AI hub in SAP AI Core Calculator to estimate usage.
  • How is data security handled and where does my data go?
    SAP does not allow model providers to train on your data. SAP has contractual agreements with model providers (like OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, etc.) ensuring that customer prompts and completions are not used to train or fine-tune their models. All LLM calls are proxied through SAP AI Core / Generative AI hub.

One model on this platform deserves particular attention: SAP-RPT-1.5, the Relational Pre-trained Transformer. It is planned to become generally available with GenAI Hub 2607a, scheduled for July 20. The dedicated session explained why this matters: while LLMs are powerful for language-based tasks, they are not designed to work with tables. Real-world ERP, CRM, and SCM tables are typically not part of standard LLM training data. In addition, LLMs cannot reliably reason numerically across columns, which increases the risk of inaccurate or fabricated values when they are uncertain. This is unacceptable for financial and operational decisions. Rewatch SAP-RPT-1: The SAP Foundation Model for Structured Data to learn about the six adoption scenarios for SAP-RPT-1 that are planned to go live in the coming months. Most importantly, start testing with the free playground at rpt.cloud.sap.

Answer to your most asked questions:

  • When is RPT-1.5 generally available and what happens to RPT-1?
    RPT-1.5 is scheduled for GA in July 2026. RPT-1 deprecation is not yet scheduled and there will be sufficient migration time, and switching is straightforward as the APIs are almost identical.

The day closed with the very first virtual CodeJam "Build code-based AI Agents" where you learned in a training system how to build state-of-the-art AI agents using Generative AI hub, Python and LangGraph. You gained the skills to create custom tools for your agents, including leveraging SAP's RPT-1 model and deploying your agents to BTP. Rewatch Build code-based AI Agents and access all materials on GitHub to get hands on yourself anytime.

Day 1 set the foundation. Day 2 put it into practice. Day 3 gave you the tools to build it. Continue with the full series:

entry.title: SAP Doesn’t Have to Win the AI Race. It Just Has to Own the Toll Booth.
entry.content:
*The views expressed here are my own personal views and doesn't represent any entity.

Every vendor on earth has “launched an AI strategy” this year, usually consisting of a chat window bolted onto the login page and a press release with the word “agentic” in it four times. So let’s be blunt about where SAP actually sits in this fight, because we need to pivot as fast as we can.

THREE PLAYERS walk into the AI market

The geniuses with no memory. Open AI, Anthropic, Google, AWS model have dazzling reasoning, but zero clue what your cost center hierarchy looks like or why Finance still does that one manual journal entry every month that everyone’s afraid to touch. Ask a foundation model to close your books and it will confidently make something up. That’s not a flaw, it’s just not what it’s for.

The CONSULTANTS with a WHITEBOARD

Databricks, Palantir Foundry brilliant at taking your data from wherever it lives and building you a beautiful ontology on top of it. Palantir has in built business ontology data models but it may take time for it to be ERP twin. The catch is that someone still has to build the ERP ontology.

That someone is expensive, that someone is you or that someone is currently a systems integrator billing by the hour.

The one who already knows where everything is filed. SAP. Thirty years of encoded business logic about what a valid purchase order actually is, who’s allowed to approve it, and what happens if you try to post to a closed period. Nobody else in this fight starts here. This is the actual moat, and it’s the one thing you cannot vibe-code your way into.

So what is Joule, actually, and why isn’t it just “SAP’s Copilot”

Copilot-style assistants live in the UI. Joule lives in the process. A generic assistant helps you ask about a purchase order. Joule agents are scoped to actually execute the P2P, O2C, or R2R process with the approval matrix, segregation-of-duties controls, and audit trail already wired in, because they’re not layered on top of the transaction, they’re native to it.

It doesn’t need to be taught your business. It was raised in it. Ask Chat GPT to create a purchase requisition and it needs you to explain your entire approval hierarchy first, every single time, in a prompt. Joule already knows, because the process metadata is the S/4 data model, not a paragraph you typed at 6pm. It fails safely, on purpose.

A generic agent hallucinating a number into a live GL posting is a finance controller’s cardiac event. Joule’s guardrails aren’t a bolt-on safety feature they’re the reason it’s allowed anywhere near a transaction at all.

Joule Studio is the tell. SAP isn’t selling you one clever chatbot, it’s giving you a factory for building process-scoped agents on your own clean-core extensions. That's a fundamentally different product bet than “here’s a really good general assistant, please supply your own guardrails.”

In short, everyone else is trying to get close enough to your business to be useful. Joule doesn’t have to get close. It’s already inside the building, holding the keys.

The real play - SAP as the context provider, not just the agent builder

Here’s the bit that gets missed because “Joule” is the sexier headline i.e. SAP doesn’t actually need every agent in your enterprise to be Joule. It needs every agent Joule, Copilot, some homegrown thing your innovation team built over a weekend to have to come through SAP to get anything real done. That’s a much bigger and much quieter ambition than “we also have a chatbot now.” Ain't it?

The BIG ELEPHANT in the room - SAP API Policy

This is what the API Policy (v4, 2026) is actually for, and why it matters more than the marketing suggests. It’s not a technical housekeeping exercise about which endpoints are deprecated. It’s SAP drawing the border around what “released” means i.e. which interfaces are governed, versioned, and safe for an external agent to call, versus what’s custom code nobody should be pointing an autonomous system at. In an agentic world, that release boundary is the trust boundary. An external LLM calling an ungoverned custom BAPI isn’t “innovative,” it’s an incident waiting for an ID number.

If we join the puzzle pieces right :

SAP becomes the toll booth for AI that needs to be right
Clean core defines what’s stable enough to expose.
The API policy defines the contract for exposing it i.e. the governed surface any agent, SAP’s or not, has to respect.
BDC defines how that context gets harmonised with data that lives outside SAP. Joule is simply the first, best-positioned tenant of all three i.e. not the whole strategy.

That reframe matters commercially. If SAP wins as “the best agent,” it’s competing head-on with Open AI and Anthropic Copilot on model quality, a fight it can’t cleanly win. If SAP wins as “the only trustworthy source of business context and process truth that any agent has to be granted access to,” it’s not competing with the model layer at all i.e. it’s charging rent to it.

The uncomfortable PIVOT - the toll booth doesn’t help if agents drive around it

Here’s the trap in the toll booth metaphor. A toll booth only works if the road actually goes through it. And right now, S/4HANA’s road was built for a human clicking through Fiori screens i.e. not for an agent that wants to skip the screen entirely and go straight for the API, the table, the data. That’s the real threat, and it’s not from Open AI. It’s structural.

If an agent can get everything it needs i.e. the data, the process context, the ability to act through a clean, governed API, then the application layer of S/4HANA, the actual ERP-as-software-you-use, becomes optional.

You’ve spent thirty years building the best-organised filing cabinet in the world, and the agent just wants to open the drawer itself. Congratulations, you’re now very expensive middleware.

So “own the toll booth” only survives if S/4HANA stops being a system people operate and becomes a system agents transact through by necessity and it means SAP has to reinvent the core, not just wrap it in AI branding. From screens to services. Fiori apps were built to be looked at.

Agents don’t look at anything. If the only path to “valid business action” is still a human-shaped UI workflow, agents will find the shortest ungoverned path around it i.e. custom tables, side databases, shadow IT with better UX and SAP loses the very control it’s trying to sell.

From batch processes to live process state. A lot of S/4’s process logic still assumes a human is waiting for the next screen. Agentic execution needs process state to be query able and actionable in real time, not “come back after the nightly job.”

From one system of record to a defensible system of judgment. Judgment as a callable capability, not bury it in ABAP that nobody can explain.

Governance has to move from “who clicked approve” to “which agent, acting under whose authority, did what.” Today’s audit trail assumes a human identity behind every action. An agent-native core needs an entirely different permission and audit model, or the first real incident undoes the trust argument SAP is selling.

Skip this reinvention and the toll booth quietly becomes a museum i.e. beautifully governed, fully compliant, and increasingly irrelevant, because the traffic found a bridge.

Where SAP is, uncomfortably, still exposed

None of this works if your SAP estate is a decade of bespoke ABAP held together with hope, which statistically it is. Clean core is the precondition for all of the above, and most clients aren’t there yet.

The real QUESTION

It’s not “can SAP out-reason GPT.” It never was. It’s “can SAP make proximity to the transaction more valuable than proximity to the model” and that bet only pays off if clean core adoption moves faster than the competition’s whiteboard.

If you're ready to retire the legacy-code dinosaur instead of polishing it with a sponge, we'd love to help chart a Clean Core roadmap that transforms complexity into AI foundation in our SAP App Haus. Please reach out to us SAP AppHaus | Deloitte UK for a face to face conversation!

entry.title: Where Your AI Agent Will Fail First: a Field You Never Touched
entry.content:
Beyond SAP Core, post 2

We recently ran a generative AI documentation tool against one of our core processes, and the output was impressive: clean process descriptions, correct object references, accurate flow diagrams. Technically, nothing looked wrong.

However, it was also useless. All because it omitted the single most important business rule in that specific process. Not because of a defect or something. The tool read everything there was to read. The rule simply isn't written anywhere: not in the code, not in the data dictionary, not in the customising and much less in any document. It lives as a naming convention inside a standard field, and in the heads of the people who have been decoding it for fifteen years, and some of those people are not even part of the company anymore.

In the first post of this series I argued that agent readiness and Clean Core readiness are two different lists. This post is about the failure mode that tops the agent list while never appearing on the Clean Core list at all: semantic drift, when a standard field stops meaning what SAP thinks it means.

Anatomy of a smart key

Let's look at a classic example of hiding business logic in plain sight. Take a standard field like a Profit Centre, and watch how it breaks down.

2 0 0 0  B  P V  3
└─┬──┘  ┬  └┬─┘  ┬
  co.   site prod. seq.
  code       line

2000 is the company code. B is the plant. PV is the product line. The last digit is a sequence number. Every character means something.

You won't find this structure in a domain definition or a check table. You definitely won't find it in a document. It lives entirely in substring operations scattered across reports and interfaces. It is in offset logic, selection screen string patterns, and institutional memory.

The field itself remains 100% standard. No modifications. No appends. Zero custom Z-objects. This is exactly why a Clean Core assessment will never flag it.

The part that makes it worse

The painful truth is that SAP already has a tool for this. Class types, characteristics, hierarchies: the standard classification system was sitting there the whole time. Nobody used it.

This happens through a predictable sequence. First, a simple gap in knowledge. Someone needed a quick fix and didn't know the standard existed. Then, fear takes over. The convention works, and changing it feels too risky. Finally, scale. The workaround grows until fixing it requires a massive, unappealing migration project.

There is a fourth stage, and it is the one nobody writes about: normalisation. After enough years, nobody sees it anymore. The convention is simply how things are.

It starts as an oversight. It scales into a structural dependency. Once a system runs on a workaround long enough, that workaround just becomes the architecture.

The number

We have found about 310 objects so far relying on positional logic for this single field. "So far" carries a lot of weight here.

The count isn't the worst part. The real issue is that these are not all custom code. Standard objects carry the exact same dependency through customising. You will find derivation rules, substitutions, and validations parsing character strings out of this field. Once standard customising relies on a hacked field, this is no longer technical debt. It is a core business dependency.

Why nothing catches it

Run your standard checks. Everything will pass.

  • ATC and custom code checks: Pass. There is no technical deviation.
  • Functional testing: Pass. The system does what the business wants. That is exactly the problem.
  • AI-generated documentation: Fails silently. It only reads what is written. This logic was never written down.

Point an AI agent at this system now. The data dictionary tells the agent it is looking at an opaque ID. The agent trusts the dictionary. The eight characters of hard-coded business meaning remain completely invisible. The agent won't throw an error. It will confidently reason about a "profit centre" while the business is actually dealing with plants and product lines.

Semantic drift is invisible to code-reading tools because the drift isn't in the code. It is in the meaning.

The only thing that caught it was a new pair of eyes

The documentation tool missed the rule because it was never written. We missed it for a different reason: we had stopped seeing it.

Recently someone senior joined the company. Strong SAP background, no exposure to any of our conventions. Within days they looked at that field and asked the obvious question: why is it like this, and is there no way to avoid using a standard field for this?

Nobody had asked that in years.

Here is the part I keep thinking about. That person read the field exactly the way an agent reads it, with no institutional memory, going by what the data dictionary says it is. The difference is that they asked. An agent will not ask.

The way out: it is not a choice between two options

People usually frame this as a choice: build a workaround view now, or run a proper migration to standard classification. That framing is a trap. You have to do both, in a strict order.

First, write the unwritten rule. Build a CDS view that breaks down the key. Parse the positions once, centrally. Project them as clean, annotated fields that any API or agent can read. This is not just another workaround. You are finally transcribing tacit business knowledge into machine-readable data. It takes days of effort, and it immediately removes the agent's blind spot.

Second, stop the bleeding. Once you map the logic, freeze it. Our development guidelines ban any new positional parsing of this field, and all new consumption should go through the CDS view.

I have to be honest about where we actually are with that. Today nothing enforces it. The rule is written down and dormant. Everyone has lived with the convention for so long that nobody flags it in a review anymore, which is precisely how the count keeps growing. Automating the check is the obvious next step. Right now it depends on someone remembering, and that is not a control.

Third, migrate as a business program. Standard classification remains the end goal. This is a multi-year effort. It requires a business sponsor. An IT architecture team cannot drive a massive refactoring of reports and interfaces alone. The CDS view stays alive until the last consumer migrates. A bridge without a demolition date is just a permanent workaround.

The question I'd actually like answered

Every older SAP system has at least one of these. A completely standard field masking a structure only the veterans understand.

Which one is yours? And how is your AI agent ever going to figure it out?

Previous in this series:   Your Agent Learned SAP From the Manual. Your System Didn't.
Next: rule sovereignty, when the logic works perfectly and no API will ever admit it exists.

entry.title: Exploring the Latest SAP Document AI Enhancements: AI, Gmail Integration, and Flexible Email Process
entry.content:
Introduction

SAP Document AI continues to enhance intelligent document processing by introducing capabilities that simplify document onboarding, improve email-based automation, and provide greater flexibility for enterprise integrations. New release focuses on reducing manual effort, streamlining configuration, and enabling organizations to build more intelligent and scalable document-processing solutions.

In this blog, we'll explore four key enhancements introduced in this release:

  • AI-powered document type detection and automatic schema generation
  • Gmail support for inbound email ingestion
  • Configurable email content processing
  • Flexible synchronous and asynchronous outbound processing

1. AI-Powered Document Type Detection and Automatic Schema Generation

One of the standout enhancements in this release is the ability for SAP Document AI to automatically identify a document type and generate a corresponding schema using artificial intelligence.

The Challenge

When onboarding a new document type, users previously needed to manually define:

  • Document Type
  • Schema
  • Schema Version

This required prior knowledge of the document structure and additional configuration before any processing could begin.

What's New?

SAP Document AI now introduces the "Use AI to fill out the document type and schema details" option during document upload.

When enabled, the solution automatically:

  • Detects the document type based on the uploaded content
  • Generates an AI-recommended schema
  • Creates the initial field structure for extraction

This allows users to begin processing documents much faster with minimal manual setup.

Business Benefits

  • Accelerates onboarding of new document types
  • Reduces manual configuration effort
  • Simplifies proof-of-concept implementations
  • Enables business users to get started quickly without extensive technical knowledge
  • Speeds up AI model adoption across departments

Example

Imagine receiving a new supplier invoice format that has never been processed before. Instead of manually creating a schema, SAP Document AI analyzes the document, identifies it as an invoice, and generates a suitable extraction schema automatically. This enables organizations to start validating and extracting data almost immediately.

 

2. Gmail Support for Inbound Email Ingestion

Email remains one of the most common channels for receiving business documents such as invoices, purchase orders, contracts, and employee forms.

To simplify document ingestion, SAP Document AI now supports Gmail accounts as inbound channels using secure OAuth authentication.

What's New?

Organizations can now connect Gmail mailboxes directly to SAP Document AI, allowing incoming emails and attachments to be processed automatically without manual uploads.

Common scenarios include:

  • Supplier invoices
  • Customer contracts
  • Purchase orders
  • HR onboarding documents
  • Support requests with attachments

Business Benefits

  • Secure OAuth-based authentication
  • Native integration with Gmail accounts
  • Fully automated email-based document ingestion
  • Reduced manual monitoring of shared mailboxes
  • Faster processing of incoming business documents

This enhancement is particularly valuable for organizations that rely on Google Workspace as their enterprise email platform.

3. Configurable Processing of Email Content

Not every incoming email should be processed the same way. Some organizations need to analyze the complete email, while others only require specific attachments.

To address this, SAP Document AI now offers configurable processing behavior for inbound email content.

What's New?

Administrators can choose how incoming emails are handled.

Option 1: Process the Entire Email

The complete email—including its content—is processed as a single document.

This approach works well for scenarios such as:

  • Customer support requests
  • Approval emails
  • Service requests
  • General correspondence

Option 2: Process Email Body and Attachments Separately

The email body and each attachment are processed independently.

For example, consider an email containing:

  • A Purchase Order attachment
  • An Invoice attachment
  • Additional processing instructions in the email body

Each component can now be routed and processed separately, enabling more accurate document handling.

Additional Enhancement

Attachments can also be processed directly using a selected Schema Version, eliminating the need to configure a workflow beforehand.

Business Benefits

  • Greater flexibility in email processing
  • Improved handling of multi-document emails
  • Simplified configuration for attachment processing
  • Better support for diverse business scenarios

4. Flexible Outbound Processing with Configurable Response Modes

Integrating SAP Document AI with downstream business applications often requires different processing approaches depending on the business scenario.

To provide greater flexibility, outbound channels now support configurable Response Modes.

Asynchronous Processing (Default)

In asynchronous mode, SAP Document AI sends the request to the target system and continues processing without waiting for an immediate response.

This mode is ideal for:

  • High-volume document processing
  • Enterprise integrations
  • Background workflows
  • Long-running processing tasks

Synchronous Processing

In synchronous mode, SAP Document AI waits for the target application to respond before completing the processing cycle.

This approach is beneficial when:

  • Immediate confirmation is required
  • Real-time business validations are needed
  • External APIs return instant processing results
  • Business processes depend on immediate downstream responses

Business Benefits

  • Supports both real-time and background processing scenarios
  • Greater flexibility for enterprise integrations
  • Improved control over outbound communication
  • Better alignment with different business process requirements

Organizations can now select the response mode that best matches their integration architecture and operational needs.

Conclusion

Recent  SAP Document AI release introduces meaningful enhancements that make intelligent document processing even more powerful and user-friendly. AI-driven schema generation reduces onboarding effort, Gmail integration simplifies document ingestion, configurable email processing offers greater flexibility, and new outbound response modes improve integration with enterprise applications.

Together, these capabilities help organizations accelerate automation, reduce manual effort, and build scalable, AI-powered document processing solutions on SAP Business Technology Platform.

As businesses continue to embrace intelligent automation, these enhancements further strengthen SAP Document AI as a key service for modern document-centric business processes.

entry.title: The Great SAP Reshuffle: Will AI Agents Eat Your SAP Career, or Just Your Coffee Breaks
entry.content:
*The views expressed here are my own and doesn't really represent any entity

A field guide for Functional, Technical, BTP, Integration, Data, Basis, and Enterprise Architecture folks who'd like to still have a job in 2030 and maybe even a better one! 

Current Scenario

Somewhere in an SAP project right now, a Business Analyst is writing a functional spec by hand, a Basis admin is manually applying a support pack at 2 AM, and an Integration Consultant is debugging an IDoc that failed for the 47th time this month.

Meanwhile, an AI agent is quietly watching all three of them and thinking"cute."

AI agents aren't coming for SAP jobs like a wrecking ball. They're coming like a very competent new hire who never sleeps, never asks for a raise, and reads the entire OSS note database for fun. The real story isn't "humans vs. agents" and it's who reinvents fast enough to become the agent's boss instead of its understudy. Let's go role by role.

SAP Functional Consultant (FI/CO, MM/SD, HR, etc.)

Junior Today: Writes config docs, runs SPRO clicks, sits in workshops taking notes nobody reads, tests the same scenario 40 times because "the business changed their mind again".

Senior Today: Owns the process design, negotiates between IT and Finance who both think they're right, and has a mental map of every custom Z-table that will ruin someone's Tuesday.

What Agents will do: Config-by-prompt is already real. "Set up a new cost center hierarchy for the EMEA entity" will become a sentence, not a sprint. Agents will draft functional specs, generate test scripts, run regression tests overnight, and flag config drift automatically.

What stays Human: Business judgment. An agent can configure a pricing procedure; it can't sit in a room and figure out why Sales and Finance have been quietly at war since 2019, or why "the system is wrong" actually means "the process is wrong and nobody wants to admit it." Change management, stakeholder trust, and translating ambiguous human politics into unambiguous system logic still is very much a people sport.

Junior Evolution: Stop being a "clicker." Become a prompt-and-validate specialist i.e. someone who can direct an agent, sanity-check its output against real business rules, and spot when it's confidently wrong (agents hallucinate config just as happily as they hallucinate anything else).

Senior Evolution: Move from "process expert" to "AI process governor" defining guardrails, owning exceptions, and becoming the escalation point when the agent's elegant solution breaks a 15-year-old business rule nobody documented.

SAP BTP Development Consultant

Junior Today: Writes ABAP and Java or Python Code, tweaks CDS views, debugs dumps, copies code from Stack Overflow with the serial numbers filed off and pulls his hair in debugging.

Senior Today: Designs the extension architecture, decides clean-core vs. "we'll deal with it later," and is the only person who understands why that one enhancement spot is held together with hope.

What Agents will do:Code generation is already table stakes. Joule and friends can write ABAP, CDS, and RAP scaffolding faster than a junior dev can open Eclipse. Agents will generate boilerplate extensions, suggest clean-core-compliant patterns, auto-document code, and even propose refactors. Debugging simple dumps and syntax errors is agent territory but complex ones?

What stays human: Architectural taste. Someone still has to decide what to build, not just generate the fastest way to build it. Performance tuning on genuinely gnarly custom logic, security-sensitive extensions, and "should we even build this or is there a standard way" judgment calls remain human turf.

Junior Evolution: Your job isn't "write code" anymore but it's "supervise the code-writer." Learn to read AI-generated ABAP/CDS critically, understand why clean-core matters, and get fluent in prompting for architecture-compliant output instead of copy-pasting whatever comes back.

Senior Evolution: Become the clean-core enforcer and platform strategist i.e. deciding what belongs in BTP, what agents can auto-generate safely, and building the guardrails (naming conventions, extension governance, security policies) that keep 50 AI-assisted developers from turning the landscape into spaghetti at machine speed.

SAP BTP Integration Consultant

Junior Today: Builds point-to-point interfaces, maps fields, watches iFlows fail because someone renamed a field in S/4 without telling anyone and fixes it with his deep technical skills.

Senior Today: Designs the integration strategy, decides API-first vs. legacy middleware, and is the human equivalent of a UN peacekeeper between SAP and NON-SAP systems and people that refuse to speak the same language and negotiates contracts with other suppliers and third parties.

What Agents will do: Field mapping, interface scaffolding, error-pattern detection, and "why did this iFlow fail" root-cause analysis are extremely automatable i.e mapping logic is basically a giant pattern-matching problem, which is an AI's favorite kind of problem. Expect agents to self-heal common integration failures (retry logic, auto field remapping on schema drift) before a human even gets paged.

What stays Human: Designing the integration landscapei.e deciding what should be event-driven vs. batch, what's an API product vs. an internal plumbing job, and negotiating data contracts between business units who each think their system is the "source of truth."

Junior Evolution: Stop being the mapping and coding guru. Learn QA and API design principles, event-driven architecture, and how to supervise self-healing integration agents across all systems rather than manually babysitting iFlows in just SAP BTP.

Senior Evolution: Become an agent integration architect-in-training even before the title i.e owning API Agents, governance, data contracts, and the "who's allowed to auto-heal what" policy that keeps autonomous agents from making landscape-wide decisions unsupervised.

SAP Data Consultant

Junior Today: Cleans master data, runs LSMW/BODS/Syniti/SNP loads, reconciles spreadsheets, and silently judges whoever built the data model they inherited.

Senior Today: Designs data governance, owns the data model strategy, and translates "our data is a mess" into an actual remediation plan.

What agents will do: Data profiling, cleansing, deduplication, and anomaly detection are practically an AI love language i.e pattern recognition at scale is exactly what these models are built for. Expect agents to auto-detect data quality issues, propose cleansing rules, and even auto-generate migration mappings between legacy and S/4 data models.

What stays Human: Data meaning. An agent can tell you 40,000 customer records have inconsistent formatting; it can't tell you which of your three "customer" definitions the CFO actually cares about, or that "clean" data that violates a regulatory requirement is worse than messy data. Governance, ethics, compliance, and cross-functional data ownership disputes stay firmly human.*

Junior Evolution: Move from "the person who fixes the spreadsheet" to "the person who defines the rules the agent uses to fix the spreadsheet." Learn data governance frameworks and get comfortable auditing AI-driven cleansing logic.

Senior Evolution: Become the data trust officer and the human who signs off on what an autonomous agent is allowed to touch, especially around master data that feeds financial reporting or compliance processes. This is a growth role, not a shrinking one.

SAP Basis / Infrastructure Consultant

Junior Today: Applies patches, monitors jobs, SAP Notes, Installations, restarts things, gets paged at 3 AM for a full disk that could've been caught by literally any monitoring tool.

Senior Today: Designs and Sizes the landscape, plans upgrades, manages performance and DR strategy, and has strong opinions about backup windows.

What Agents will do: This is arguably the most automatable role in the entire SAP universe. Patch application, job scheduling, performance monitoring, capacity forecasting, and routine troubleshooting are exactly the kind of "detect pattern, apply known fix" work agents excel at. Autonomous Basis agents that self-patch, self-tune, and self-heal in hyperscaler environments aren't science fiction i.e they're a 2026 roadmap slide.

What stays Human: Architecture decisions (on-prem vs. RISE vs. hyperscaler-native), security strategy, and the judgment call of "should we actually apply this patch to production during peak season" I.E a question that requires understanding business context an agent doesn't have. Also being accountable when it breaks. Someone's name still needs to be on the change ticket.

Junior Evolution: This is the loudest wake-up call of the bunch. "I know how to monitor and all the T-codes for system monitoring" stops being a career. Junior Basis folks need to move fast into automated cloud infrastructure, security, and automation orchestration and becoming the people who build the self-healing systems, not the people the self-healing systems replace.

Senior Evolution: Shift from "landscape operator" to "landscape architect and risk owner" i.e deciding what autonomy agents get, setting security and compliance boundaries, and owning the business continuity conversation that no agent gets to have unsupervised.

SAP Solution/Enterprise Architect

Junior today: Doesn't really exist as a title as this is an earned role, usually arriving after a decade of scars from the roles above.

Senior today: Sets the technology strategy, aligns SAP roadmap with business strategy, makes the "buy vs. build vs. extend" calls, and is the person the CIO calls when a decision is above everyone else's pay grade.

What Agents will do: Scenario modeling, TCO analysis, business and ROI case generation, landscape documentation, and even generating first-draft architecture options ("here are 3 ways to integrate this acquisition's ERP") and agents will make EAs faster and better-informed, crunching analysis that used to take weeks into hours.

What stays Human: Everything that requires actually deciding, under uncertainty, with organizational politics, budget constraints, and career-risk attached. Enterprise Architecture is fundamentally a trust and judgment role and someone has to own the consequences of the call, and boards don't yet accept "the agent recommended it" as an answer.

Evolution: The EA role doesn't shrink as it becomes the command center for AI governance across the whole SAP landscape. EAs increasingly own the meta-question every other role above is wrestling with i.e what should agents be allowed to decide, and what must always come back to a human? This is quickly becoming one of the highest-value, most human-proof roles in the entire ecosystem i.e. provided the person in it actually understands how the agents work, not just what they output.

The Punchline! How Not to Get Outsmarted by Your Own Tools

Here's the uncomfortable joke at the center of all this,the SAP ecosystem spent 30 years building the most exhaustively documented, rules-based, pattern-heavy body of enterprise knowledge on Earth which makes it spectacular training data for AI. We basically built the machine that automates us, one OSS note at a time.

Stop competing with agents on speed and volume. You will lose. Compete on judgment, context, and accountability instead.
Learn to supervise, not just execute. The new core skill across every SAP role is "prompt it, review it, catch what it got wrong." Treat every AI output like a very smart intern's first draft i.e talented, fast, occasionally confidently insane.
Move up the ambiguity ladder, continuously. Whatever task just became "prompt-able," that's your cue to move one layer up in judgment, not to defend the task.
Get fluent in governance, not just execution. Knowing how to configure something matters less than knowing whether it should be configured that way and who's accountable when it isn't.

What capabilities organizations need to build?

AI governance muscle, Clear rules for what agents can decide autonomously vs. what needs human sign-off, per role and per risk level (a Basis agent patching a sandbox ≠ a Basis agent patching production finance).

Human-in-the-loop checkpoints designed on purpose, not bolted on after an incident i.e. especially in Basis, Integration, and Data, where autonomous agents will move fastest.

A culture that rewards catching the agent being wrong, not just shipping fast. The team that blindly trusts AI output will out-ship everyone right up until the day it doesn't.

entry.title: How We Brought Transparency to Our AI Activities: A Practical Approach to Tracking and Coordinating
entry.content:
Too many AI initiatives, not enough visibility. We achieved transparency, clear ownership, and faster delivery with a simple approach. A shared Kanban board in Microsoft Teams as the operational backbone, plus a lean management summary for decision-making. The result: fewer duplicates, clearer accountability, and better throughput.

The problem: Many initiatives, no shared picture. If you need to check Excel files, Jira boards, Teams chats to answer “How many AI initiatives are running right now?”, you’re not alone. We saw the same pattern repeatedly: information scattered across tools and teams, unclear ownership, hidden blockers, and no reliable reporting for leadership. In workshops, one question kept surfacing: “Is someone already working on this use case?” Surprisingly often, nobody knew. As the number of ideas, pilots, and implementations grew, the lack of a consolidated view began to slow down execution and obscure progress.

 

Why AI initiatives need dedicated coordination AI doesn’t fit neatly into traditional project boxes. It cuts across S/4HANA, Ariba, Datasphere, Signavio and beyond. Teams are cross-functional, and the underlying AI portfolio evolves continuously. Without a shared overview, it’s easy to duplicate efforts, bury valuable knowledge in silos, and starve leadership of the signal they need to make prioritization decisions. Coordination becomes the bottleneck. That led us to a simple question: How can we make every AI activity visible—without adding yet another project management tool?

 

Our Solution: A Teams Kanban Board for AI Activity Management

Instead of introducing another complex application, we decided to leverage a tool that everyone was already using every day: Microsoft Teams.

By creating a dedicated AI Activities Kanban Board, we established a single source of truth for all AI-related initiatives—from the first idea through productive deployment.

Operationally, the board changed the rhythm of collaboration. Teams now have a single place to see what’s in flight, what’s blocked, and who is accountable. Stand-ups focus on movement between columns rather than gathering status. Duplicate work shows up early. And because the board is embedded in the tools people already use, the barrier to adoption is low: no new logins, no new training, just a clear and shared way of working.

 

Beyond the Board: Reporting for Management and Stakeholders

The board is a working tool for the team. Management needs something different: condensed, decision-ready information. That is why we built a Management Summary on top of the board — structured into three sections:
 
1. Overview — A status distribution across all phases, the current Top 3 priorities (e.g., Deduction & Dispute Agent, Sales Order Creation Agent, Joule for Consultant), and AI unit consumption against the contracted budget.

2. Efficiency Metrics — Four indicators that answer whether we are getting faster and better: completed tasks, average cycle time, current work in progress, and a 6-month WIP trend. 

3. Outlook — Upcoming milestones and the backlog broken down by category (Joule, Embedded AI, Custom AI, AI Agents) to support prioritization decisions.

 

How It All Connects

The Kanban Board is the living, daily working tool. From it, we export data regularly and generate the Management Summary, either as a PowerPoint deck or through Power BI dashboards for automated reporting. Additional context (e.g., strategic commentary, risk flags) is added manually where needed. This ensures that:
  • The project team has a real-time collaboration tool.
  • Management receives condensed, decision-ready reports without needing to interpret raw board data.

 

Final Thoughts

AI initiatives move fast — and that pace is only accelerating. The approach described here is deliberately simple: a Kanban Board as the operational backbone, and a lean reporting structure to bridge the gap to management. No heavy tooling, no lengthy rollout. What it does require is discipline — keeping the board alive, reporting consistently, and treating transparency not as a reporting obligation but as a governance principle.
If you are currently managing AI activities in spreadsheets, email threads, or informal conversations, this might be the right moment to take a step back and set up a structure that scales with your ambitions.
I am happy to discuss further or share experiences — feel free to leave a comment or reach out directly.

entry.title: SAP Document AI: Simplifying External System Integration with the External Call Node
entry.content:
Introduction

In today’s intelligent document processing scenarios, extracting information from a document is only one part of the automation journey. The real business value comes from what happens after the data is extracted.

For example, an invoice can be processed by SAP Document AI, but the extracted invoice number, vendor, amount, or other metadata may then need to be sent to an external application, validated against another system, or used to trigger a downstream business process.

This is where the External Call node in SAP Document AI workflows becomes particularly useful.

The External Call node enables a Document AI workflow to communicate with external systems and APIs using HTTP requests. It can retrieve information from an external API or send extracted document information to another application for further processing.

What is the External Call Node?

The External Call node allows an SAP Document AI workflow to make an HTTP request to an external system.

The communication is handled through an outbound channel, which provides the connection details required to communicate with the target system, including:

  • Base URL
  • Authentication
  • Connection settings

The External Call node can be used with HTTP GET and POST requests.

A simplified flow looks like this:

Document → SAP Document AI → Extraction → External Call → External System → Response → Next Workflow Step

This makes the External Call node useful for extending Document AI beyond document extraction and connecting it with broader business processes.

Common Use Cases

There are several practical scenarios where the External Call node can be used.

1. Sending extracted invoice data to another system

Suppose SAP Document AI extracts:

  • Invoice number
  • Vendor name
  • Invoice date
  • Net amount
  • Tax amount
  • Total amount
  • Currency

The workflow can send these values to an external application using a POST request.

For example:

{
  "documentId": "${documentClassifier.fetchValue("documentType")}",
  "documentNumber": "${invoiceExtraction.fetchValue("documentNumber")}",
  "invoiceDate": "${invoiceExtraction.fetchValue("documentDate")}",
  "vendorName": "${invoiceExtraction.fetchValue("vendorName")}",
  "totalAmount": "${invoiceExtraction.fetchValue("totalAmount")}",
  "currency": "${invoiceExtraction.fetchValue("currency")}"
}

The receiving system could then create an invoice record, trigger validation, or start another business process.

2. Retrieving information from an external system

The External Call node can also be used with a GET request.

For example, after extracting a vendor ID from an invoice, the workflow could call an external API to retrieve additional vendor information.

The workflow could then use the response in subsequent workflow steps.

Document AI Extraction
        ↓
Extract Vendor ID
        ↓
External Call – GET
        ↓
External Vendor API
        ↓
Vendor Information
        ↓
Condition / Validation
        ↓
Next Workflow Step

Configuring an External Call Node

Before configuring the External Call node, at least one active outbound channel must be available in SAP Document AI.

The channel defines how SAP Document AI connects to the external system.

Once an active channel is available, the External Call node can be configured with the following parameters.

1. Identifier

The Identifier is mandatory.

It is the technical name of the workflow node and can later be referenced when accessing the node's outputs.

For example:

externalCallNode_1

2. Label

The Label is optional and is primarily used to provide a meaningful description for the node.

For example:

Get Vendor Details

Using meaningful labels can make complex workflows easier to understand and maintain.

3. Channel ID

The Channel ID is mandatory.

This determines which outbound channel is used for the HTTP request.

The selected channel provides the:

  • Base URL
  • Authentication details
  • Connection configuration

For example, you might configure a channel pointing to:

https://api.example.com

and then use the External Call node to append a specific API path.

If the selected channel is inactive when the workflow is executed, the External Call will fail.

4. URL Suffix

The URL Suffix is optional and allows you to append an additional path or query string to the channel's base URL.

For example:

/api/users/123

You can also dynamically construct the URL using workflow expressions.

Static URL

/api/users/123

Dynamic URL

/api/invoices/${invoiceExtraction.fetchValue("invoiceNumber")}

Query parameters

/search?query=${invoiceExtraction.fetchValue("vendorName")}

This makes it possible to use values extracted by Document AI dynamically when calling external APIs.

Important consideration

SAP Document AI does not automatically URL-encode or escape values resolved from expressions.

Therefore, values inserted into query parameters should be appropriately URL-encoded.

The URL Suffix also does not allow certain characters, including:

< > \ ^ ` |

Curly braces must be used correctly when expressions are involved.

5. HTTP Method

The HTTP Method is mandatory.

The supported methods described for the External Call node are:

  • GET – typically used to retrieve information
  • POST – typically used to send data to an external system

The default method is:

GET

The Payload Data field becomes available when POST is selected.

6. Success Status Codes

The Success Status Codes parameter determines which HTTP responses should be considered successful.

The default configuration is:

2xx

This means any 2xx HTTP response is treated as successful.

You can also specify individual status codes or combinations.

For example:

200,201

This accepts HTTP 200 and 201.

Another example:

2xx,3xx

This accepts both successful and redirect responses.

A particularly useful scenario is:

200,404

For example, if the workflow checks whether a record exists in an external system, both 200 and 404 might be valid business outcomes rather than technical failures.

If the returned HTTP status code does not match the configured success codes, the workflow follows the error-handling path.

7. Payload Data

The Payload Data field is available for POST requests.

It defines the JSON body sent to the external system.

For example:

{
  "name": "John Doe",
  "age": 30
}

The real power comes from combining static JSON with Document AI workflow expressions.

For example:

{
  "documentNumber": "${invoiceExtraction.fetchValue("documentNumber")}",
  "vendorName": "${invoiceExtraction.fetchValue("vendorName")}",
  "totalAmount": ${invoiceExtraction.fetchValue("totalAmount")}
}

This allows extracted document information to be passed directly to an external API.

Be careful with data types

When building JSON dynamically, pay attention to whether the extracted value is a:

  • String
  • Number
  • Boolean
  • Object
  • Array

For example, a string should normally be represented as a JSON string, while a boolean or number should not unnecessarily be surrounded by quotation marks.

SAP Document AI validates the JSON structure in real time, which helps identify malformed payloads before execution.

Understanding External Call Outputs

One of the most useful aspects of the External Call node is that its response can be consumed by downstream workflow nodes.

The node exposes two important methods:

getStatusCode()

and

getResponseJson()

getStatusCode()

The getStatusCode() method returns the HTTP status code received from the external system.

Example:

externalCallNode_1.getStatusCode()

If the API returns:

200

the expression evaluates to:

200

This can be particularly useful in a Condition node.

For example:

externalCallNode_1.getStatusCode() == 200

The workflow can then take different paths depending on the result.

getResponseJson()

The getResponseJson() method returns the response body as a JSON object.

For example, suppose the external API returns:

{
  "id": "12345",
  "data": [
    {
      "name": "Item A"
    },
    {
      "name": "Item B"
    }
  ],
  "timestamp": "2026-04-02T10:30:00Z"
}

The workflow can navigate through this response using .get() and .item().

Accessing a JSON Field

To retrieve the id:

externalCallNode_1.getResponseJson().get("id")

Result:

"12345"

Accessing an Array

To retrieve the complete data array:

externalCallNode_1.getResponseJson().get("data")

Accessing an Array Element

Array indexes are zero-based.

Therefore:

externalCallNode_1.getResponseJson().get("data").item(0)

returns:

{
  "name": "Item A"
}

To retrieve the name:

externalCallNode_1.getResponseJson().get("data").item(0).get("name")

Result:

"Item A"

This provides a convenient way to consume API responses without having to process the complete JSON manually.

Important: ${} vs Expression Syntax

One detail that is easy to miss is how expressions are written depending on where they are used.

URL Suffix or Payload Data

When embedding an expression inside a string or JSON payload, use:

${externalCallNode_1.getResponseJson().get("id")}

Expression-only fields

For fields such as a Condition Expression, use the expression directly:

externalCallNode_1.getStatusCode() == 200

Understanding this distinction helps avoid expression configuration errors.

CSRF Considerations

Another scenario to be aware of is an error while relaying the request to the destination.

This can occur when the target system does not correctly support or handle CSRF tokens.

If this happens, verify whether the receiving system supports the required CSRF mechanism and review the outbound channel configuration.

This becomes particularly relevant when integrating Document AI with enterprise applications that enforce CSRF protection.

 

Key Takeaways

The External Call node in SAP Document AI provides a straightforward way to integrate document-processing workflows with external APIs and applications.

The most important points to remember are:

  • An active outbound channel is required.
  • The channel provides the base URL, authentication, and connection configuration.
  • GET can be used to retrieve information.
  • POST can be used to send JSON data.
  • URL Suffixes can contain dynamic workflow expressions.
  • Payload Data supports dynamic values using workflow expressions.
  • Success Status Codes can be customized.
  • The default timeout is 30 seconds.
  • getStatusCode() provides the HTTP response status.
  • getResponseJson() provides access to the JSON response.
  • .get() can be used to retrieve JSON fields.
  • .item() can be used to access array elements.
  • Responses can be reused in downstream workflow nodes.
  • URL and JSON values are not automatically encoded or escaped, so the data must be formatted correctly.

Conclusion

SAP Document AI is not limited to extracting information from documents. With workflow capabilities such as the External Call node, extracted information can be connected to external APIs and downstream applications, enabling more complete end-to-end automation.

For organizations building invoice, purchase order, supplier, or other document-centric processes, this capability provides a practical way to connect document intelligence with business applications and automation workflows.

The key idea is simple:

Extract the information, call the right system, process the response, and continue the business process.

That is where document processing starts becoming true end-to-end automation.

entry.title: Connecting SAP Integration Suite with SAP Document AI and SAP Business AI
entry.content:
From Email to Intelligent PO Review on SAP BTP

 

Gmail -> SAP Integration Suite -> SAP Document AI -> SAP AI Core / GPT-5-mini -> SAP Integration Suite (Extension = Flask -> SAP HANA Cloud -> Review Dashboard)

The final flow receives PDF purchase orders by Gmail, pulls them via Cloud Integration mail sender adapter, extracts them with SAP Document AI, validates them with GPT-5-mini through SAP AI Core, and displays the response Json on MPL of Integration suite.

[Extension - stores them in SAP HANA Cloud, and routes low-confidence POs to manual review. No S/4 posting is performed in this guide]

[Extension will not be covered here and are just ideas or may be on a next blog   😊]

INFO: Blog focus

This article is deliberately centered on connectivity: Gmail -> SAP Integration Suite -> SAP Document AI -> SAP Business AI through SAP AI Core / generative AI hub. No S/4 posting is performed here.

 

SECURITY: Public-blog safe

Passwords, client secrets, OAuth tokens and private service key values are omitted. Use the field names and patterns shown but keep actual credentials only in SAP BTP / Integration Suite secure stores.

 

1. Why I Built This

Many customers still send purchase orders as PDF attachments. The difficult part is not merely extracting text; it is connecting the full enterprise chain in a governed way: receive email, identify the PDF, call a document extraction service, validate the result with a foundation model, apply a quality rule and further as extension may be to show those in dashboard.

 

2. Prepare Gmail: Alias, Filter, Label and IMAP Access

2.1 Create a Gmail plus-alias

No second mailbox is required. Gmail plus-addressing lets you receive mail at an address such as your.autual-email-id+cpi_po@gmail.com while it still arrives in your normal mailbox.

  1. Take your existing Gmail user name before the @ sign.
  2. Append +cpi_po before @gmail.com. Example: your.name+cpi_po@gmail.com.
  3. Use that alias as the PO address for test senders or customers.
  4. Integration Suite must authenticate with the real Gmail mailbox address, not the + alias.

INFO: Why use an alias

The alias gives you a deterministic filter key without creating another mailbox. Google documents filtering by Gmail aliases, including +category patterns.

 

2.2 Create label CPI_PO and the Gmail filter

  1. In Gmail, create a new label named CPI_PO.
  2. Click Show search options in the Gmail search box.
  3. In To, enter your +cpi_po alias email id.
  4. Optionally restrict the filter with has:attachment filename:pdf.
  5. Choose Create filter.
  6. Select Apply the label -> CPI_PO.
  7. Do not choose Mark as read; the iFlow selects unread mail.
  8. Send a PDF test mail and confirm it appears under label CPI_PO.

To: your.name+cpi_po@gmail.com
Has the words: has:attachment filename:pdf
Action: Apply label CPI_PO
Do not: Mark as read

 

 

User-supplied Gmail view: incoming PO mail is visible under the CPI_PO label.

2.3 Authentication used in this demo

  1. Enable Google 2-Step Verification.
  2. Create a Google App Password for the integration. Google App Passwords are 16-character passcodes and require 2-Step Verification.
  3. In Integration Suite, store the real Gmail address and App Password in a User Credentials artifact named GMAIL_PO_MAIL.

SECURITY: Production note

The working demo uses IMAPS + Plain User Name/Password protected by TLS. SAP also supports OAuth2 Authorization Code for IMAP4. For a production blog follow-up, OAuth is the preferred modernization path.

 

3. Provision the SAP BTP Foundation

The build uses SAP BTP Cloud Foundry with a dev space. Service plans and exact UI labels can differ by commercial agreement, region and trial generation, so use the plan available in your tenant while preserving the same capabilities.

5. Connect SAP Business AI: SAP AI Core, Generative AI Hub and GPT-5-mini

  2. Create a service key.

5.2 Connect SAP AI Launchpad to AI Core
