  2. Add/select the SAP AI Core runtime connection using the service key.
  3. Select resource group default.
  4. Open the Generative AI Hub / model catalog or the foundation-models scenario.

5.3 Make GPT-5-mini available

In the working tenant, GPT-5-mini was available through the foundation-models scenario. Model availability is tenant, region and plan dependent, so select GPT-5-mini only if it is present in your model catalog.

  1. Choose the foundation-models scenario and the OpenAI / Azure OpenAI executable available in your tenant.
  2. Select GPT-5-mini.
  3. Create a configuration/deployment for resource group default.
  4. Wait until the deployment is Running/healthy.
  5. Copy the deployment URL or deployment id.

INFO: SAP governance layer

The generative AI hub is a capability of SAP AI Core and SAP AI Launchpad. It provides governed access to supported foundation models while SAP AI Core remains the runtime/lifecycle foundation.

GPT-5-mini is used as a validator, not as the source of extracted PO values. The prompt asks for strict JSON containing decision, qualityScore, missingFields and reason.

 

6. Create Integration Suite Security Material

7. Build the Final Integration Flow

Create an Integration Flow named Email PO to Document AI plus GenAI. Add sender Gmail and receivers DocumentAI, AICoreGPT. Create a local integration process named Poll Document AI.

7.2 Step 1 - Get PDF Attachment

Add a Groovy Script step named Get PDF Attachment. It selects the first PDF attachment, moves the PDF bytes into the body, and stores the file name in a header.

def attachments = message.getAttachments()
def pdf = attachments.find { name, handler ->
    name?.toLowerCase()?.endsWith(".pdf") ||
    handler?.getContentType()?.toLowerCase()?.contains("application/pdf")
}
if (pdf == null) throw new Exception("No PDF attachment found")
message.setBody(pdf.value.getInputStream().bytes)
message.setHeader("POFileName", pdf.key)

 

7.3 Step 2 - Build Document AI multipart request

BuildMultipart.groovy creates the multipart/form-data payload containing the PDF and extraction options.

options = [

]

7.4 Step 3 - POST Document AI

7.5 Step 4 - Store the Document AI job id

def json = new JsonSlurper().parseText(message.getBody(String))
if (!json.id) throw new Exception("Document AI did not return a job ID")
message.setProperty("DocAIJobId", json.id.toString())
message.setProperty("DocAIPending", "true")

 

7.6 Step 5 - Poll until DONE

  1. Create local process Poll Document AI.
  2. Add HTTP GET to /document/jobs/${property.DocAIJobId}?extractedValues=true.
  3. Add Groovy status check.
  4. Loop while ${property.DocAIPending} contains true.
  5. Maximum iterations: 15.
  6. Wait five seconds between PENDING polls.

if (status == "DONE") {
    message.setProperty("DocAIPending", "false")
} else if (status == "PENDING") {
    message.setProperty("DocAIPending", "true")
    sleep(5000)
} else {
    throw new Exception("Document AI processing failed: " + status)
}

 

7.7 Step 6 - Normalize PO JSON and calculate Document AI score

CreateCleanJson.groovy maps headerFields / lineItems to the application contract. The demo uses a deliberately conservative rule: Document AI quality is the minimum confidence across extracted header and line-item fields.

if (score <= 1.0) score = score * 100.0
...

...

vendorName: fieldValue(headers, "vendorName")
subtotal: fieldValue(headers, "subtotal")

 

WARNING: Why some scores look low

A single weak field can force Manual Review. In one real test, vendorName confidence was 47.8%, so the complete PO was intentionally routed to review even though other fields were above 90%.

 

7.8 Step 7 - Build the GPT-5-mini review request

aiRequest.groovy saves the normalized PO in OriginalPOJson, then requests strict JSON using response_format/json_schema.

{
  "decision": "ACCEPT | REVIEW",
  "qualityScore": 0-100,
  "missingFields": ["..."],
  "reason": "..."
}

Header: AI-Resource-Group = default

7.10 Step 9 - Merge AI review and final score

The corrected Groovy sets finalScore = min(Document AI score, GenAI score). If GPT explicitly returns REVIEW but the numeric score is >=90, the score is capped at 89 so the business route remains Manual Review.

if (docScore != null && aiScore != null) {
    finalScore = Math.min(docScore, aiScore)
}
if ("REVIEW".equalsIgnoreCase(decision) && finalScore >= 90.0) {
    finalScore = 89.0
}
finalScore = Math.round(finalScore * 10.0) / 10.0

 

WARNING: Groovy parser gotcha

Keep the rounding statement on one line. A failed version broke before / 10.0 and produced: expecting '}', found "Flask".

 

7.11 Step 10 - Log the final JSON

showResult.groovy adds Final_PO_AI_Result.json to the message log. This is invaluable for troubleshooting without exposing secrets.

 

8. Run the End-to-End Test

  2. Confirm it appears under label CPI_PO and remains unread until the iFlow polls it.
  3. Wait for Integration Suite to process the message.

entry.title: What a Second Document AI Workshop Taught Me About Governance
entry.content:
A few days ago we published a recap of the second edition of our SAP Document AI workshop, hosted together with SAP. Nearly fifty people joined, from energy, manufacturing, construction, food and consumer products, technology, and industrial services. The recap covers what you would expect a recap to cover: the standard invoice schema, custom schemas, ingestion options, confidence levels, the ROI exercise.

That recap does what a recap should: it records what we covered. This one is about what we were asked, which turned out to be a different list. Going back through the session afterward, the questions clustered somewhere I hadn't anticipated. Not extraction accuracy, not which document types are supported, not how the schemas work. The longest single exchange of the day was about retention, storage location, and data classification, one participant asking one question after another, each narrowing further on the same thing.

That is what I want to write about, because I think it says something about the distance between what we prepare and what people need to know before they can say yes.

The questions

It started simply enough. During the demo, files were being dropped into a monitored folder for processing, and someone asked whether that folder gets cleaned up afterward. Easy answer: yes, the file is removed after processing.

But the follow-up came immediately, and then another, and then another. Is the data stored for future analytics? Since this is SaaS, is it stored on your side or on SAP’s side? And then, after a slightly confused exchange where we weren’t sure whether the question was about the demo environment or the product itself, the participant reframed it in the way that finally made it land:

From a security point of view, where would the data be stored?

That reframing is the part I keep thinking about. We had answered the first version of the question twice already, correctly, and it hadn’t helped. Because "does the folder get cleaned up" and "from a security point of view, where does the data live" are not the same question, even though the first is a subset of the second. We were answering at the level of the demo, and he was asking at the level of an audit.

The actual answers, once we got there: the source file is deleted after processing. The extracted data lives in the flow, with a decommissioning period after which it is destroyed. That period is configurable in the Document AI administration settings, and — this is the part that mattered most to the room — it is meant to follow your company’s rules. If your policy says thirty days, you set thirty days. If it says ninety, you set ninety. One organization in our earlier proof of concept needed five years of traceability, so that is what was configured.

The answer was not a number

Here is what I did not appreciate until afterward. He was not asking for a specification, he was asking who holds the pen. And the answer — that retention is a configuration governed by your own policy, not a fixed property of the product — is a genuinely different kind of answer than a number would have been. It moves the question from "is this product compliant" to "is your policy applied," which is a question the customer answers, not the vendor.

I think that is why the exchange took so long. We kept offering product facts to someone who was trying to work out where a responsibility boundary sits. Both parties were being reasonable, but we were answering different questions. If I run this session again, that framing goes on a slide: the boundary. Here is what SAP operates, here is what you configure, here is what remains your policy decision.

The question that decides the scope

One question from that same thread has stayed with me longer than the rest, and I don't think it has a short answer. Can a file be classified at the point of upload? If a document is marked confidential rather than general business data, can that marking travel with it and govern how it's handled downstream?

Undoubtedly, that question is different from the rest. It isn't asking what the tool extracts, it's asking whether a governance attribute can survive a pipeline, and that is what decides whether a document workflow stays limited to invoices and delivery notes or can be pointed at regulated material. Most of the automation conversation happens on one side of that line. Whether you can cross it is a different evaluation entirely, and it's the one I'd want to run early rather than late, because it changes which use cases are even on the table.

If you've implemented classification-driven handling in a Document AI workflow, or decided you couldn't and routed around it,  I'd like to hear how you approached it.

"Document AI is not a translator"

The other theme I did not expect came up twice, from two different participants, in two forms that sound similar and are not. The first: a shared services operation in the U.S. receives forms from China in Mandarin. Does extraction work on the Mandarin document, and can the output come back in English?

Extraction across languages, yes. Translation, no; and the clearest thing said all session was that Document AI is not a translator. It reads what is on the page. What happens to that text afterward is a workflow decision, and if the workflow needs translation, the workflow can translate.

The second version arrived later and looked like the same question, but wasn’t. A document is uploaded in English; the person reviewing it is logging in from a LATAM country and wants to read it in their own language. That is not extraction at all. The document is stored as it is; what you are asking about is a translation service sitting alongside the process, which on BTP means pointing at SAP Translation Hub.

Two questions, one distinction: the language a document arrives in, and the language a person works in. They kept getting merged in the room, and I suspect they get merged in requirements documents too.

Where things live

In the post I wrote after the first edition of this workshop, I ended on a question about Clean Core: where should new capabilities live?

I did not plan for the second edition to rhyme with it. But the loudest question in that room was, almost word for word, where does the data live? I think it is the same question, one layer further down. Deciding where innovation happens is an architecture conversation. Deciding where the data sits, how long it stays, and whose policy governs it is the conversation that has to follow, and it is the one that actually determines whether anything reaches production.

Both editions of this workshop taught me something I did not go in expecting. The first taught me that Clean Core is less a restriction than a decision about placement. The second taught me that placement is not only a question about code.

entry.title: Generative AI-Powered Document Processing in SAP Integration Suite
entry.content:
Introduction

What if SAP Integration Suite could understand a PDF document instead of simply processing it?

Invoices, sales orders, and other business documents are often received as PDF attachments with different layouts and formats. Traditional document processing relies on predefined templates and parsing rules, which can be difficult to maintain.

In this blog, we build an end-to-end Generative AI document processing scenario in SAP Integration Suite. Using Claude as a practical example, we classify PDF documents, extract key business data, and use the structured result to route and process the document in SAP Cloud Integration (CPI).

We will also cover validation, human approval, exception handling, and key enterprise considerations when processing sensitive business data with Generative AI.

Business Scenario

The scenario is based on a shared business mailbox used to receive documents from customers and suppliers. Incoming emails can contain different types of PDF business documents, such as invoices and sales orders.

SAP Cloud Integration receives the email and extracts the PDF attachments. Each document is then sent to a Generative AI model, which identifies the document type and extracts the relevant business fields.

Based on the AI result, CPI can route the document to the appropriate processing flow. For example, an invoice can be prepared for an SAP S/4HANA supplier invoice process, while a sales order can be prepared for the sales order creation process.

Example document types:

  • Supplier Invoice
  • Customer Sales Order
  • Purchase Order
  • Unclassified / Unsupported Document

Example end-to-end flow:

[Diagram: End-to-end Generative AI document processing flow from email PDF attachment through SAP Cloud Integration and Generative AI to classification, data extraction, validation and downstream SAP processing]

The objective is to move from document-specific parsing logic to a more flexible approach where the AI model can understand different document layouts while SAP Cloud Integration remains responsible for orchestration, validation, mapping, routing, and integration with downstream SAP systems.

Building the SAP Cloud Integration Flow

The integration flow starts when an email containing one or more PDF attachments is received. Each PDF is processed independently by the Generative AI pipeline before the result is made available for further business processing.

The main processing steps are:

  1. Extract PDFs into Collection — extracts the PDF attachments from the email and prepares them for processing.
  2. Process Multiple PDF Attachments — uses a General Splitter to process each PDF independently.
  3. Prepare the Document Data — retrieves the file name and PDF content of the current document.
  4. Build GenAI Request — creates the SAP Generative AI Hub Orchestration request containing the prompt, document, tools and selected model.
  5. Call the Generative AI Service — sends the request through the AI Receiver Adapter.
  6. Process the AI Response — converts and processes the returned structured response.
  7. Router — determines the appropriate processing path based on the AI classification.

[Screenshot: Complete SAP Cloud Integration iFlow showing email intake, PDF extraction, document splitting, Generative AI processing, response handling and downstream routing]

The complete iFlow shows how Generative AI is incorporated into a conventional SAP integration process while keeping the integration and business processing logic within SAP Cloud Integration.

Extracting PDF Attachments

The first step is to extract the PDF attachments from the incoming email and prepare them for further processing. Since a single email can contain multiple documents, the integration flow collects all PDF attachments into a single XML structure.

The Groovy script reads the attachments, filters out non-PDF files, converts each PDF from binary content to Base64, and stores the result together with the original file name.

 

import com.sap.gateway.ip.core.customdev.util.Message
import groovy.xml.StreamingMarkupBuilder
import groovy.xml.XmlUtil
import java.util.Base64

def Message processData(Message message) {
    def attachments = message.getAttachments()
    def builder = new StreamingMarkupBuilder()
    def xml = builder.bind {
        attachments {
            attachments.each { fileName, dataHandler ->
                def contentType = dataHandler.getContentType()
                if (contentType?.toLowerCase()?.startsWith("application/pdf")) {
                    def pdfBytes = dataHandler.getInputStream().bytes
                    def pdfBase64 = Base64.encoder.encodeToString(pdfBytes)
                    file {
                        fileName(fileName)
                        fileContent(pdfBase64)
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    }
    message.setBody(XmlUtil.serialize(xml))
    return message
}

[Code Snippet: Groovy Script – extracting PDF attachments, filtering PDF files, converting the content to Base64 and building the attachment collection]

The resulting message body has the following structure:

<attachments>
    <file>
        <fileName>invoice_001.pdf</fileName>
        <fileContent>BASE64...</fileContent>
    </file>
    <file>
        <fileName>sales_order_002.pdf</fileName>
        <fileContent>BASE64...</fileContent>
    </file>
</attachments>

This collection is then passed to the next step, where a General Splitter processes each PDF independently. This allows multiple documents received in the same email to follow the same Generative AI processing logic without combining them into a single AI request.

Processing Multiple PDF Attachments

When an email contains multiple PDF documents, the General Splitter processes each document independently. The splitter uses the XPath expression /attachments/file to create a separate message for every <file> element in the collection.

In this example, Parallel Processing is disabled and Stop on Exception is enabled, ensuring that documents are processed sequentially and that an exception stops the overall processing.

[Screenshot: General Splitter – XPath expression /attachments/file, with parallel processing disabled and Stop on Exception enabled]

Each split message then continues through the same processing logic, starting with retrieving the file name and PDF content before sending the document to Generative AI.

Preparing the Document Data

After the splitter creates an individual message for each PDF, a Content Modifier is used to extract the document content and file name from the current XML element.

The values are stored as exchange properties, file_content and file_name, and will be used to populate the corresponding fields of the Generative AI request.

[Screenshot: Content Modifier – extracting the current PDF file name and Base64 content into exchange properties]

Building the Generative AI Request

The Build GenAI Request Content Modifier creates the JSON payload that will be sent to SAP Generative AI Hub. The request follows the SAP Generative AI Hub Orchestration format rather than a provider-specific API format.

SAP Orchestration V2 defines the request around the config, modules and prompt_templating sections, together with placeholder_values for dynamic values. The complete request structure is documented in the SAP Help Portal – Orchestration Workflow V2.

This harmonized interface provides access to multiple foundation models through a consistent orchestration interface rather than requiring CPI to call a provider-specific API. SAP describes Orchestration as providing unified access to multiple generative AI models through consistent code, configuration and deployment. See the SAP Help Portal – Orchestration for more information.

In this example, Claude is selected as the foundation model. The request contains the prompt, the PDF document, the available tools for document classification and field extraction, and the selected model.

[Screenshot: Build GenAI Request – beginning of the SAP Generative AI Hub Orchestration request]

[Screenshot: Build GenAI Request – prompt and message configuration]

[Screenshot: Build GenAI Request – tool definitions used for document classification and field extraction]

[Screenshot: Build GenAI Request – selected Claude model and completion parameters]

[Screenshot: Build GenAI Request – remaining request configuration and tool-calling settings]

The PDF is passed dynamically using a placeholder. The actual Base64 content of the current document is taken from the CPI exchange property file_content:

[Screenshot: Content Modifier – dynamically inserting the current PDF Base64 content into the Generative AI request]

The {{?pdf_base64}} placeholder is resolved at runtime using the file_content exchange property. This allows the same request structure to be reused for every PDF processed by the splitter.

For PDF input, SAP Orchestration supports a multimodal content item using type: file and file_data. The PDF can be supplied as Base64 data or, where supported, as a URL. The exact documented representation is available in the SAP Help Portal – Templating documentation.

The model parameters depend on the selected foundation model. For example, SAP documents max_completion_tokens as required for Anthropic models.

The classification tools used in this example follow the tool-calling mechanism provided by SAP Orchestration. Multiple tools can be defined, allowing the model to select the appropriate function based on the document and the tool definitions. See the SAP Help Portal – Tool Calling documentation for more information.

Calling the Generative AI Service

The next step is the AI Receiver Adapter, which sends the prepared request to SAP Generative AI Hub. In this example, the adapter uses the Orchestration - Completion operation.

[Screenshot: AI Receiver Adapter – Orchestration Processing configuration]

Orchestration provides a harmonized interface between SAP Cloud Integration and supported foundation models. The integration flow sends the Orchestration request, while SAP manages the interaction with the selected foundation model.

In this example, the request specifies an Anthropic Claude Sonnet model together with parameters such as the maximum completion tokens and tool-choice behaviour.

The AI Receiver Adapter is responsible for the connection and execution of the Orchestration request, rather than defining the prompt or document-processing logic itself.

[Screenshot: AI Receiver Adapter – connection configuration using OAuth 2.0 client credentials, AI resource group and orchestration deployment]

The connection uses an OAuth 2.0 client credential configuration stored in the SAP Cloud Integration security material. The orchestration deployment and AI resource group are configured in the adapter's Processing settings.

Demo: Classifying and Routing a Sales Order

With the integration flow in place, we can test the scenario using a sales order PDF. The document in this example is an ABB Australia Sales Order Acknowledgement, with sales order number 10099324 and a total order value of AUD 3,239.63.

[Screenshot: Sales Order PDF – example document submitted to the Generative AI processing flow]

After the PDF is sent to Generative AI, Claude identifies the document as a Sales Order and calls the route_sales_order tool. It extracts the order number, customer, date, total amount, currency and number of line items.

[Screenshot: Claude Response – Sales Order classification, selected tool and extracted business data]

The response is then converted from JSON to XML so that it can be processed by standard CPI steps.

Routing the Document

The CPI Router checks the extracted tool name using an XPath expression:

/root/content/name = 'route_sales_order'

If the condition is true, the message follows the Sales Order route. The corresponding Message Mapping transforms the extracted data into the structure required by SAP S/4HANA.

[Screenshot: CPI Router – XPath condition checking for the route_sales_order tool]

The same pattern can be extended to other document types, such as invoices, purchase orders, and unclassified documents.

Demo: Classifying an Invoice

To demonstrate that the same approach can handle different document types, we can use an invoice PDF as a second example.

The document is an invoice issued by GlobalTech Manufacturing GmbH to Nordic Retail Solutions AB. It contains a typical invoice structure, including an invoice number, invoice date, sales order reference, line items, VAT, and total amount due.

[Screenshot: Invoice PDF – example invoice submitted to Generative AI]

After the document is submitted to Generative AI, Claude successfully identifies it as an invoice and selects the corresponding route_invoice tool. The response contains the extracted invoice number, vendor name, total amount, invoice date, due date, and currency.

[Screenshot: Claude Response – Invoice classification, selected tool and extracted invoice data]

This example demonstrates that the model can identify the document type and extract the relevant business information even though the document has a different structure from the Sales Order used in the previous example.

Human Approval Before Posting

Identifying a document and extracting its business data is only one part of the process. In a real enterprise scenario, the AI result should not necessarily lead directly to the creation or posting of a business document in SAP S/4HANA.

For example, a sales order identified by Generative AI could be prepared for creation in S/4HANA, but a business user may first need to review the extracted information and approve the transaction. The same principle can be applied to invoices and other financially relevant documents.

This introduces a human-in-the-loop step between AI-based document processing and the final business transaction:

PDF → Generative AI → Classification & Extraction → Validation → Human Approval → SAP S/4HANA

The approval step can be implemented using workflow capabilities available in SAP S/4HANA or through an additional approval application or process on SAP BTP.

This approach also separates two different responsibilities. Generative AI is responsible for understanding the document and extracting the relevant information, while the business user remains responsible for the final business decision.

Depending on the business risk and validation requirements, the process can be designed in different ways. Low-risk, highly predictable documents could potentially be processed automatically, while documents above a defined value threshold, documents with missing or inconsistent information, or documents requiring a business decision could be sent for manual approval.

Example control flow:

  • AI classification and extraction – identify the document and extract the relevant fields.
  • Business validation – check mandatory fields, values, customer or supplier information, and other business rules.
  • Approval – a designated business user reviews and approves or rejects the proposed transaction.
  • S/4HANA processing – after the required approval is obtained, the business document can be created or posted.

This provides a practical balance between automation and control. The AI can remove much of the manual effort involved in reading and entering information from PDFs, while the business retains control over the final transaction.

Handling Sensitive Business Data

One of the most important considerations when introducing Generative AI into document processing is data protection. Business documents can contain confidential commercial information, personal data, financial information, customer details, bank account information, and other data that an organisation may not want to send to an AI service.

For example, an invoice may contain supplier and customer information, addresses, payment details, bank account information, and transaction values. A sales order can contain customer information, product details, prices, quantities, and other commercially sensitive data.

Therefore, the question is not simply whether Generative AI can technically process the document. The organisation must first determine whether the document is allowed to be processed by the selected AI service and model.

SAP Generative AI Hub provides an enterprise-managed layer for accessing and orchestrating foundation models. SAP Orchestration also provides capabilities such as content filtering and data masking, which can be incorporated into an orchestration workflow where appropriate. See the SAP Help Portal – Orchestration documentation for details.

However, these capabilities do not remove the customer's responsibility for data protection. SAP documentation explicitly cautions users not to store personal data in prompts. A production implementation should therefore consider applicable privacy requirements, data classification, data residency, contractual requirements, and the organisation's internal policies before enabling real business documents for AI processing.

For this reason, a production implementation should include a data classification and security decision before the document is submitted to Generative AI.

For example, the integration could distinguish between:

  • Approved documents – documents that are permitted to be processed by the selected AI service and model.
  • Sensitive documents – documents that require masking, minimisation, or additional controls before AI processing.
  • Restricted documents – documents that company policy does not allow to be submitted to the selected AI service and therefore require an alternative processing mechanism.

This can be implemented as an additional control before the AI Receiver Adapter:

PDF → Data Classification → Security Check → Generative AI / Alternative Processing

Where possible, data minimisation should also be considered. If the AI model only needs specific information to classify the document, unnecessary personal or confidential information should not be included in the AI request.

Conclusion

This example demonstrates how Generative AI can extend SAP Cloud Integration beyond traditional rule-based document processing. Instead of building separate parsing logic for every document layout, the integration can use a foundation model such as Claude to understand the document, identify its type, and extract the relevant business information.

At the same time, SAP Cloud Integration remains responsible for the integration logic. It manages the incoming documents, controls the processing flow, validates the AI result, routes the document, and transforms the extracted information into the structures required by SAP S/4HANA.

For a production implementation, AI-based document processing should be combined with appropriate business validation and, where required, human approval before creating or posting business documents. Data protection is equally important: organisations should determine which documents and data are permitted to be processed by Generative AI and apply the appropriate security and privacy controls.

The result is a flexible integration pattern in which Generative AI provides document understanding, SAP Cloud Integration provides orchestration and integration, and business processes remain in control of the final transaction.

This approach can be extended beyond invoices and sales orders to other business documents and processes, while continuing to use the same core integration pattern.

entry.title: Why Our First Document AI Exercise Was a Résumé, Not an Invoice
entry.content:
A few weeks ago our team ran the second edition of our SAP Document AI workshop together with SAP, with fifty people participating. I did not attend, but afterwards I went through the exercises that our people had prepared, mostly out of curiosity about how they had decided to teach the tool. I assumed the first exercise would be an invoice. It is a résumé, and the invoice only turns up later on.

I was surprised to say the least. Every business case for document automation that I have ever seen starts with invoices, purchase orders and delivery notes, because those are the documents that arrive in volume and cost real money to process by hand. Starting anywhere else looked like a detour. Reading through the exercises properly, I realised the order was deliberate, and working out why has changed how I look at these projects.

The reason is that a résumé is a much harder document than an invoice, even though it feels like the opposite. An invoice does have structure. A company receiving supplier invoices might see fifty different layouts across its vendors, but each of those layouts is stable in itself. The vendor name is always in the same place on invoices from that vendor, and the total is always where the total goes. Résumés have no equivalent to that. There is no standard anyone follows, so every candidate decides for themselves how to order things and what to leave out, and two résumés for the same position can look almost nothing alike. That is what makes it useful for teaching, because it takes away the possibility of solving the problem the old way.

With traditional OCR the way you deal with fifty invoice layouts is to upload all fifty and show the system where every field sits in each one. You are annotating positions on a page, which means the intelligence of the system is really in the mapping, and the mapping is work that never finishes. Every new supplier with a new layout is another template that somebody has to build and then maintain. SAP Document AI works differently, because the extraction is done by language models rather than by position matching. In the workshop exercises nobody annotates anything and nobody tells the system where on the page to look. You describe what you are after, and the description is what does the work. With a résumé you have no way around learning that properly. With an invoice you can carry on believing you are still doing field mapping and never notice the difference.

Writing the instructions

What that description looks like in practice is the part I found most interesting, because it is easy to agree with the idea that you describe the fields without appreciating how much judgment goes into it. At the level of the whole schema, the exercise asks participants to write something like this:

You are an experienced senior recruiter who is preparing information for your hiring director. Check every field carefully and make sure all the information is extracted accurately. Make sure the analysis works even though you have a variety of document layouts.

There are three sentences there and each one is doing something different. The first one establishes who is supposed to be reading the document and for what purpose, which affects every decision the system makes about what matters and what does not. The second sets an expectation about care. The third one tells it not to assume consistency, and that is the sentence that separates a configuration which works on the documents you tested from one that still works on the documents you have not seen yet.

There is also a second level, because instructions can be attached to individual fields as well as to the schema. In the résumé exercise, the field for the end date of a work experience entry has an instruction telling the system to write 999 when there is no end date at all. That detail is very small and I think it taught me more than anything else in the exercise. Somebody had to sit down and think about what absence means. Extracting an end date is the easy half. The harder half is deciding what should happen when there isn't one, and what the downstream systems ought to receive so they can tell a missing date apart from a date of zero. That is a decision about how the process works, and it happens to get written into a text box.

The guidance our team gave during the session was to imagine that you are explaining to a new colleague how to read the document, and I would put it even more strongly than that. What you are writing is the procedure that a new employee would need if they had no context at all and nobody nearby to ask. All the things that normally go without saying have to be said. Even the naming of fields turns out to matter, because a field called "number" gives the system nothing to work with. It has no way of knowing whether that means a document number, a purchase order number or a quantity of something. The field name, the description of the field and the processing instructions all become part of the same context, so careless naming is not only untidy, it actually makes the results worse.

Where the real difficulty is

Somewhere around here I stopped thinking of this as a technical topic at all. The question of whether AI can read our documents accurately is more or less settled at this stage, and the answer is that it can, well enough, provided there is a review step for the cases it is unsure about. The question that is not settled, and the one that I suspect will separate the companies that get value out of this from the ones that stall halfway, is whether their people are able to describe their own processes precisely enough for a machine to follow them.

Everything in those instructions is business knowledge that somebody wrote down. Which fields matter and why, what counts as accurate, what to do when a piece of information is simply not there. In most companies that knowledge does exist, but it exists in the heads of the people who have been doing the work for years, and it has never been written down anywhere because there was never any reason to write it down. The person simply knows. What Document AI does is make that undocumented knowledge suddenly important, and companies differ enormously in how much of it they can actually put into words.

Teams that can explain their own rules tend to move quickly, because the configuration ends up being close to a transcription of what they already knew. Teams whose processes live entirely in individual judgment have a harder time, and they often put the difficulty down to the technology. Usually there is nothing much wrong with the model. They just never wrote the specification.

I should be fair to the counter-argument here, because it is a real one. SAP ships more than thirty preconfigured templates and a standard invoice schema, and for a company whose problem is supplier invoices, most of this may never come up. You copy the standard schema, activate it and you are largely done. So the difficulty I am describing is not universal. It appears when the documents are specific to your business, which in my experience is where the interesting volume tends to sit anyway, but it is worth saying plainly that a lot of companies will start with something that mostly works out of the box.

Who should be doing this

All of which raises something I do not think many companies have thought about. The instinct is to hand the task to IT, because it lives in a technical interface, inside BTP, next to the integration work that IT is doing anyway. But almost nothing I described above is technical in nature. Deciding what 999 stands for is an accounts payable decision. Deciding that a low confidence result on a high value invoice needs a person to look at it while the same confidence on a routine one does not is a decision about controls. Writing "you are an experienced senior recruiter" is an attempt to describe a job that somebody in the company actually does.

My own view is that this work belongs with the people who do the work, and that the technical teams should be supporting it rather than owning it. The alternative, where IT writes descriptions of processes that nobody in IT has ever performed, tends to produce mediocre results which then get blamed on the technology. If that is right, then preparing for a document AI project is not mainly a technical exercise at all. It is asking the people who know the work best to write down what they do, in enough detail that somebody with no context could follow it. Most companies have never asked them to do that, and it may well be the most useful thing to do first.

entry.title: SAP Document AI : Stop Building What's Already Shipped by SAP BAIP & Know the TradeOffs
entry.content:
Every enterprise deals with a mountain of documents—invoices, purchase orders, delivery notes, remittance advices, contracts, and receipts.

Today, extracting information from these documents is no longer the biggest challenge. Several platforms, including SAP, Microsoft, and Google, can already classify documents and extract structured data. Based on several discussions with my customers and experience of Invoice, PO or contract details information extraction, the question I find more interesting is:

What happens after the extraction?

That is where SAP Document AI becomes relevant, especially for organizations already invested in the SAP ecosystem.

From Documents to Business Processes

A real document automation process is much more than:

Document → Data

It is closer to:

Document → Extraction → Validation → Exception Handling → Business Process

For example, extracting an invoice number, supplier, PO number, tax, and amount is useful. But the real business value comes from validating that information, handling exceptions, and ultimately using it in an SAP business process with help of pre-delivered schemas and templates that can be reused for multiple instances.

With a standalone document-intelligence API, the extraction may be straightforward. The additional work often comes afterward—building integrations, validation logic, workflows, user review, monitoring, and support.

This is where SAP Document AI takes a broader approach.

What SAP Document AI Brings

SAP Document AI on SAP BTP combines document processing with pre-trained models, generative AI capabilities, business-data enrichment, APIs, workflows, and human review.

For common documents such as invoices, purchase orders, and payment advice, the process can include:

1. Ingestion

Documents can enter through configured channels, APIs, email-based scenarios, and SAP integration capabilities.

The objective is to bring documents into the process without creating unnecessary custom infrastructure.

2. Extraction and Validation

The service can classify documents, extract relevant fields, provide confidence information, and support enrichment with business context.

For an invoice, that could mean validating supplier or purchasing information before the transaction moves forward.

If the system is confident, processing can continue automatically. If not, it can be sent for human review.

3. Human Review and Learning

Real-world documents are messy. Suppliers change layouts, scans aren't always clean, and extraction will sometimes need correction.

SAP's Instant Learning capabilities can use corrections from business users to improve extraction for supported scenarios.

This creates a practical feedback loop:

Automation → Exception → Human Correction → Improved Automation

4. SAP Business Integration

This is ultimately where the value lives. The objective isn't simply to produce JSON. It is to move from:

Document → Validated Business Data → SAP Business Process

For organizations using RISE S/4HANA, that business-process connection can be just as important as extraction capability itself.

How Should SAP Customers Evaluate It?

I would not compare document AI platforms only on extraction accuracy or API pricing. Instead, look at the total effort required to reach the business outcome.

With a standalone extraction service, you may still need to build:

  • Email Ingestion and Business rules
  • Master-data validation and Exception handling
  • Human in-the-Loop review & Workflow
  • SAP integration + Monitoring and support

Those additional components can become a significant part of the implementation effort.

For an organization already running SAP, SAP Document AI offers the advantage of being part of the broader SAP BTP ecosystem, rather than treating document processing as a completely separate capability that later has to be connected back to SAP.

The Bigger Picture

The most important shift is this:

Document AI shouldn't be evaluated by how well it reads a document. It should be evaluated by how effectively it helps complete a business process.

Reading an invoice is useful. Getting that invoice validated, handling the exceptions, and moving it into the right SAP process is where the real business value starts.

The goal isn't more extracted data.
The goal is fewer manual touches and faster business processes.

SAP Document AI delivers a fully integrated, enterprise-grade business process out of the box. If your documents ultimately become sales orders, vendor invoices, or HR records inside an SAP ecosystem, running raw OCR on hyperscaler solutions adds architectural overhead to a solved problem.

Conclusion:

The real value of SAP Document AI goes beyond data extraction—it connects documents directly to business processes, closing the gap between AI insights and action in S/4HANA. For enterprises looking to scale intelligent document processing, the focus should be on end-to-end process automation, integration, and business value—not extraction alone.

This post explored SAP Document AI- Premium Edition architecture, the true Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) compared with hyperscaler alternatives, and the scenarios where each approach delivers the greatest value.

The takeaway is clear: successful Document AI adoption is not about extraction accuracy alone—it is about how quickly and efficiently extracted intelligence becomes part of the enterprise business process

entry.title: SAP Document AI: Extracting Information from Documents
entry.content:
Introduction:

Let’s be honest: every business handles a large volume of documents, such as vendor invoices, purchase orders, and payment advices. The key information in these files must eventually be stored in SAP systems.

In my case, I had a real requirement to capture data from PDF and document files and store it for downstream business processing. Without AI, this work is mostly manual: users read each document, identify required fields, and enter them into the system. This approach is slow, repetitive, and prone to errors.

This is where SAP Document AI helps. It automatically reads PDFs and document images, extracts the required information, and returns structured output that can be directly used in business workflows. Instead of spending time on manual data entry, teams can focus on validation and process execution.

In this blog, I will explain how SAP Document AI works, how schema drives extraction, and how this helps solve real-world document processing challenges.

SAP Document AI

SAP Document AI is an end-to-end document processing solution that extracts information from your business documents automatically. Got an invoice as a PDF? Upload it. SAP Document AI reads it, identifies the relevant fields, pulls out the data, and hands it to you in a structured format — ready to be used in your business processes. It handles both structured documents (like invoices with predictable layouts) and unstructured documents (where information could be anywhere on the page).

Supported File Types:
  • JPEG / JPG
  • PDF
  • PNG
  • TIF / TIFF

Whether your vendor sends a scanned PDF or a photo of an invoice — it can handle it.

How Does It Know What to Extract? That's Where Schema Comes In

Here's the thing: every business cares about different data points. Some companies need the tax ID, others don't. Some track payment terms, others skip it. So how does SAP Document AI know what to look for?

What is a Schema?

A schema is essentially a blueprint that describes the structure of your data  what fields you need extracted, what they're called, and what type of data they contain. You have two options: standard and custom schemas. With custom schemas, you
define your own fields and provide specific extraction details. With standard schemas, pre-built configurations are available in the dropdown — no customization needed.

Defining a Schema (Custom)

When you create a schema, you define two categories of fields:

Header Fields — Information that appears once per document:

  • Invoice Number
  • Invoice Date
  • Vendor Name
  • Total Amount

Line Items — Repeating rows of data:

  • Material Description
  • Quantity
  • Unit Price
  • Line Total

For each field, you specify:

PropertyWhat It Means
NameTechnical name of the field (e.g., `invoiceNumber`)
LabelHuman-readable name (e.g., "Invoice Number")
DescriptionWhat this field represents — helps the AI understand context
Data TypeThe type of data expected (string, number, date, etc.)
Setup TypeManual

Note: Don’t forget to activate the schema. If you do not activate it, it will not appear under the document schema list.

Setting Up a Document

Once your schema is ready, you move to the Document configuration. Here you'll find a few options:

Document Type

Choose what kind of document you're working with:

  • Invoice
  • Purchase Advice
  • Purchase Order
  • Custom(for anything else)
Schema

Select which schema to apply — only active schemas appear in the dropdown. This links your document type to the fields you want extracted.

In my implementation, I processed a vendor purchase order (PO_2026-001234).
The system extracted key fields with confidence ranging from 76% to 100%.

Here's what happened next:
• PO_Number (confidence 98%): Directly validated against existing POs
• SHIP-TO_PARTY (confidence 76%): Manually reviewed to extract customer number
• Delivery_Date (confidence 92%): Auto-filled with warning for manual date validation
• Email (confidence 88%): Auto-populated but marked for verification

entry.title: How to Use SAP Document AI in SAP Build Process Automation (BPA): A Step-by-Step Demo
entry.content:
Introduction:

If you already know what SAP Document AI is and want to see a practical integration example, this blog is for you.

For a full functional introduction, read my previous post:  SAP Document AI: Extracting Information from Documents.

In short, SAP Document AI automatically extracts structured information from business documents such as invoices and purchase orders. But knowing how it works in theory is one thing. Getting it to work reliably in a real BPA workflow is another.

In this post, I'll walk you through a practical integration—complete with what went wrong on my first attempt, which document types surprised me, and most importantly, proof that the workflow actually delivers value.

Prerequisites

Before you start, make sure you have:

  • Access to SAP BTP with the Document AI service enabled.
  • (Optional) Access to SAP Build Process Automation.
  • The necessary roles/permissions to call APIs and manage BPA projects.
Step 1: Get a Bearer Token

To call the Document AI API, you need an OAuth Bearer token.
If you’re using a configured destination in SAP BTP, you can skip this step.

Otherwise, use the following API call to get your token:

return{
    method:'GET',
    url:docurl + '/oauth/token?grant_type=client_credentials',
    responseType : 'JSON',
    resolveBodyOnly: true,
    headers: {
        Authorization: 'Basic ' + <Encoded_clientCredentials>
    },
 }

 

Tip : Encode your client ID and client secret as `client_id:client_secret` in Binary for the Authorization header.
 Step 2: Submit Your Document for Extraction

Now, you need to tell Document AI what kind of document you’re sending and which schema to use.
This is done by setting the right metadata in your request.

let documentOption = {
documentType: "custom", // or "invoice", "purchaseOrder", etc.
schemaName: "SAP_invoice_schema",
headerFields: ["purchaseOrderNumber"],
clientId: "default"
};

let payloadDocAICall = {
method: 'POST',
url: <url> + "/document-information-extraction/v1/document/jobs",
responseType: "json",
resolveBodyOnly: true,
metadataType: irpa_core.enums.request.metadataType.formData,
headers: {
Authorization: <access_token>
},
metadata: [
{
name: "file",
file: <filePath>,
},
{
name: "options",
value: JSON.stringify(documentOption)
}
],
timeout: 30000
};
return payloadDocAICall;

 

  • documentType: The type of document (e.g., "invoice", "custom")
  • schemaName: The schema you defined in Document AI

Step 3: Check the Job Status

After submitting your document, you’ll get a job ID.
You need to check the status of this job to see if extraction is complete.

let option = {
method: 'GET',
url: docAiUrl + "/document-information-extraction/v1/document/jobs/" + <your_job-id>,
responseType: "json",
resolveBodyOnly: true,
headers: {
Authorization: <your_token>,
'Cache-Control': 'no-cache'
}
};
return option;
Step 4: Poll Until the Job is Done

In your BPA workflow, use a forever loop (or a repeat-until loop) to keep checking the job status.

  • If the status is `"DONE"`, exit the loop and process the results.
  • If the status is `"PENDING"` or `"RUNNING"`, wait a few seconds and check again.

This ensures you only move forward once the extraction is complete.

Step 5: Process the Extracted Data

Once your job status is `"DONE"`, you can access the extracted fields in the response and use them in your workflow.

Error Handling
  • Always check for errors in API responses (e.g., invalid token, file not found, extraction failed).
  • If the job status returns `"FAILED"`, log the error and notify the user or take corrective action.
  • Handle timeouts and network issues gracefully by retrying or alerting the user.
Real-World Use Case

Imagine you receive 200 vendor invoices every month:

Phase 1 (Manual Entry):

  • 60 hours/month on data entry
  • 8% error rate = 16 invoices with mistakes

Phase 2 (With SAP Document AI):

  • Configure schema, test on 10 documents
  • Deploy to production with 80% confidence threshold
  • Monitor, tweak thresholds, handle edge cases

entry.title: Where Should AI Sit in an SAP Architecture? A Practical View for Enterprise Teams
entry.content:
When an enterprise decides to introduce AI into its SAP landscape, the conversation often starts with the model.

Which model should we use? Where should we host it? How do we connect it to SAP?

Those are important questions, but they come later.

The first architectural question should be more fundamental: where should AI interact with the business?

An AI capability may need access to business transactions, enterprise data, process rules, users, external applications, or several of these at once. Putting an AI model beside an SAP application does not automatically create a good enterprise architecture.

The better approach is to decide where intelligence belongs based on the business process, context, data, integration requirements, security, and level of autonomy required.

SAP's current AI-native North Star architecture takes a similar systems-level view, connecting user experience, processes, foundation capabilities, and platform services rather than treating AI as an isolated component. SAP describes the architecture as a strategic direction rather than a product specification or roadmap.

AI Is Not Just Another Application Layer

Traditional enterprise architectures tend to separate applications, data, integration, and user experience into defined layers.

AI introduces another dimension because it can reason over information, interact with users, participate in processes, and in some scenarios take actions.

That means architecture teams need to consider more than where the model runs.

They need to understand where the AI gets its context, which systems it can access, what actions it can perform, and where business controls remain in place.

Consider a simple procurement scenario. An employee asks an AI assistant about a purchase request. Answering the question may require access to the request, supplier information, approval status, purchasing policies, and possibly information stored outside SAP.

The AI therefore needs more than a language model. It needs business context.

SAP's current AI-native architecture places significant emphasis on this connection between reasoning, business data, semantics, processes, and governed execution.

Where AI Fits in an SAP Architecture

SAP's AI-native North Star architecture describes four layers that work together: User Experience, Process, Foundation, and Platform.

1. User Experience Layer

The user experience is often the most visible part of enterprise AI.

SAP's Joule provides conversational interaction with SAP capabilities and can support informational, navigational, transactional, and analytical use cases depending on the SAP solution and capability available.

This changes how users interact with enterprise applications.

Instead of navigating through several screens to locate information, a user can express an intent and receive relevant information or assistance through the available Joule capability.

But there is an important distinction between AI assistance and AI action.

An assistant explaining why an invoice is blocked is different from an AI capability initiating an action that changes a business transaction. The second scenario introduces additional requirements around authorization, process controls, auditability, and human oversight.

That distinction should remain clear during architecture design.

2. Process Layer

The process layer is where the architectural discussion becomes more interesting.

AI can interact with workflows, APIs, events, business capabilities, and agents. SAP's North Star architecture describes the process layer as evolving toward more agentic processes, where applications provide capabilities that agents can use across SAP, partner, and third-party systems.

That does not mean every workflow should become an AI agent.

A process with fixed business rules, predictable inputs, and strict approval requirements may still benefit from deterministic workflow logic.

An agent becomes more interesting when the process requires reasoning across information, handling variable situations, or coordinating several capabilities.

The architecture decision should therefore start with the process rather than the technology.

3. Foundation Layer

AI can only reason effectively when it has access to relevant context.

This is where enterprise data and semantics become important.

SAP's current architecture describes the foundation layer as the place where data and AI come together, with SAP Business Data Cloud and SAP Knowledge Graph contributing to governed, semantically grounded business context.

There is a major difference between giving AI access to data and giving AI enough context to understand what that data means.

For example, a model may retrieve a sales order, customer record, delivery status, and payment information. That does not automatically mean it understands the relationships between those objects or the business rules governing the process.

Data quality, semantics, access controls, and business context therefore become architectural concerns, not simply data-management tasks.

4. Platform Layer

The platform provides the environment where applications, integrations, agents, and workflows can operate.

SAP describes SAP Business Technology Platform as providing services across areas including data management, application development, integration, and security within its AI-native architecture.

This makes the platform layer important when an AI use case crosses application boundaries or requires custom extensions and integrations.

However, BTP should not automatically become the answer to every AI requirement.

The right architecture depends on the actual use case, existing SAP capabilities, integration requirements, data location, and operational constraints.

A Practical Conceptual Architecture

A simplified enterprise AI architecture could look like this:

User
  ↓
Joule / Application Experience
  ↓
AI / Agent Orchestration
  ↓
Business Process Layer
  ↓
SAP S/4HANA / SAP Applications
  ↓
Enterprise Data + Business Context

Across these layers, several capabilities need to operate consistently:

APIs | Events | Identity | Security | Governance | Monitoring | Human Approval

This should be viewed as a conceptual architecture, not an official SAP reference diagram.

The important point is that AI does not operate independently of the enterprise landscape. It needs controlled access to the systems, processes, and context required to complete its intended task.

Should AI Sit Close to SAP Applications?

Keeping AI close to an SAP application can make sense when the use case depends heavily on application context, business transactions, user workflows, and SAP business data.

For example, an AI capability assisting a user with information directly related to an SAP transaction may benefit from being closely integrated with that application experience.

The trade-off appears when the use case extends beyond one application.

If the AI needs information from SAP, CRM, external databases, documents, or third-party applications, the architecture needs to account for cross-system integration and consistent access controls.

This is where the architecture needs to move beyond simply asking where the model sits.

The more useful question becomes: what does the AI need to understand and what does it need permission to do?

When Should AI Sit Outside the Core SAP Application?

Some AI use cases naturally cross enterprise boundaries.

Consider a process that combines SAP transactions with CRM information, external documents, supplier data, and an organization-specific AI model.

In such a scenario, an application or integration layer can provide separation between the core business application and the AI capability.

SAP BTP is one possible architectural option for these types of extensions, depending on the requirements. SAP's current AI Golden Path is specifically intended to help architects and AI project leads select appropriate AI capabilities, data layers, and runtime services for enterprise AI applications.

The important point is not to force every AI capability into the same location.

Architecture should follow the business requirement.

Security and Governance Cannot Sit at the End

Security cannot become a final checkpoint after an AI architecture has already been designed.

AI capabilities may interact with sensitive business information and, depending on their role, may be able to initiate actions.

Architecture teams therefore need to consider:

  • Identity
  • Authorization
  • Data access
  • Agent permissions
  • Model access
  • Auditability
  • Human oversight
  • Monitoring
  • Governance
  • Guardrails

SAP's current AI-native architecture treats trust, security, ethics, and governance as concerns spanning the architecture rather than as a separate final layer.

This becomes particularly important as enterprises move from AI that answers questions toward AI that participates in business processes.

A Practical Decision Framework for Enterprise Teams

Before deciding where AI should sit, ask:

  1. What business problem are we solving?
  2. Where does the required data live?
  3. Does the AI need transaction context?
  4. Does it need to execute business actions?
  5. Which APIs or events are available?
  6. Does the process require deterministic execution?
  7. What level of autonomy is acceptable?
  8. Where should human approval remain?
  9. What security controls are required?
  10. How will the AI capability be monitored?

These questions can prevent teams from selecting an AI technology before they understand the architecture around it.

Common Architectural Mistakes

Several mistakes can make enterprise AI projects harder than they need to be.

Choosing the model before defining the use case is one.

Treating AI as nothing more than a chatbot is another. A conversational interface may be useful, but enterprise value often depends on what happens behind that interface.

Other risks include poor data quality, excessive agent permissions, bypassing existing process controls, removing human approval too early, and creating isolated AI pilots that never connect to the broader enterprise architecture.

The common thread is architectural isolation.

AI needs to operate within the enterprise context rather than beside it.

What Enterprise Teams Should Take Away

SAP's current AI direction points toward a closer relationship between AI, business context, processes, applications, and enterprise data.

For architecture teams, that means the AI model should not be the starting point.

Start with the business problem.

Then understand the data, process, context, integration, level of autonomy, and governance requirements.

Only then does the question of which AI capability or model to use become much easier to answer.

Key Takeaways

  • Architecture should come before model selection.
  • AI needs business context, not just data access.
  • Not every workflow requires an AI agent.
  • Integration and governance should be designed upfront.
  • Human oversight remains important for higher-risk actions.

Conclusion

The question of where AI should sit in an SAP architecture does not have one universal answer.

For some use cases, AI may sit close to the user experience. For others, it may participate in business processes, work with enterprise data and semantic context, or operate through platform and integration services.

The stronger architecture is the one that connects AI to the right business context while keeping process controls, security, and governance intact.

SAP's AI-native direction provides one useful architectural reference for thinking about that shift. The practical challenge for each enterprise is deciding how those principles apply to its own landscape, processes, and risk profile.
